subsubtopic: MR. CAOUETTE (CHARLEVOIX)-VETERANS LAND ACT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege prompted by the successive and contradictory statements made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) in the last few weeks. On March 7, he said to the House that he had no intention of reviewing the possible extension of the deadline applicable to the Veterans Land Act and 1 quote his own words:
In the circumstances, adherence to the lending deadline specified in the act will not represent a denial of benefits to any veteran.
A few lines above that, he clearly stated, and I quote:
I am of the opinion, therefore, that veterans sincerely interested in obtaining VLA benefits for the purposes contemplated by the act have had ample time in which to do so. Virtually every veteran-
I skip a bit of his speech and come to the sentence that I read a while ago.
After the non-confidence motion moved by the official opposition, the minister said, as is reported on page 434 of Hansard for March 12, 1974:
For many months now, together with the officials of my department, I have studied very closely the possible implications of such an extension.
And a bit further on, he added:
-I wish to further emphasize that I am quite prepared to take another look at this whole question in light of the plea made today. If, after looking at all the evidence, I can conclude that the deadline should be extended, then I would be prepared to so recommend.
Yesterday, the minister repeated this same statement in committee. Today, following a letter which I wrote to the minister on February 13, 1974, once again about the Veterans Land Act, the minister gave me the same explanations that he had given in his first speech on March 7, when he refused to consider an extension for the application of this act. Moreover, the last paragraph of the letter dated March 20, 1974 that I have received from the minister reads as follows:
I thank you for having written to me since it has given me an opportunity to review with you the various provisions of this act, and particularly to explain to you why the date of March 31, 1974 will-
There is no supposition. He says "will". This is clear enough.
-will put an end to the applications made by veterans eligible for obtaining loans to buy a property.
Mr. Speaker, I protest against such a reply which is completely discriminatory and which contradicts the statements made yesterday and on March 19 by this same minister.
I should like to obtain today from the minister either a statement or a revision of the letter which I received today, stating exactly what he intends to do, in order that he stop playing politics on this issue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. CAOUETTE (CHARLEVOIX)-VETERANS LAND ACT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION PERIOD
speechtext:
The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caouette) raised a question of privilege and submitted to the House that the minister had made statements the hon. member thinks are inconsistent. The Speaker has no other responsibility than determining whether there is a prima facie question of privilege which later on could be submitted to the House in the form of a motion. I cannot conclude that the circumstances described by the hon. member for Charlevoix warrant a debate under Standing Order 17. I call the hon. member's attention to citation 113 of the fourth edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and I quote:
A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in Parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the House power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy.
The hon. member for Charlevoix may have a grievance against the minister, but I suggest that he could raise the matter during the proceedings, either in the House or in committee, or ask an oral or written question. I repeat that I do not think the rules or practice of the House allow to settle a matter by raising a question of privilege.

First report of Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs-Mr. Jerome.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF FURTHER INCREASE IN PRICES OF BREAD AND MILK-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do have the report of the Food Prices Review Board on bread and obviously I have read it more closely than did my hon. friend. As I said, I have received a preliminary report from the Bakery Council which indicates that its members do not intend to make increases beyond present levels unless they can make a case before the Food Prices Review Board that cost increases are such as to warrant further price increases. I think I would want to get firm and definite information as soon as possible today before giving further indication of the need for government response in this very important matter. ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
I do not begrudge the minister the praise which he has received. He at least had the courage to admit to the people of Canada that the present transportation policy in this country is a failure. However, I want to emphasize that in my view the people of Canada ought not to be beguiled by this honest and frank confession by the minister. The people of Canada have to remember that it was a Liberal government in 1966 and 1967 which proposed this policy which the minister now finds to be a failure. Indeed, this minister was a member of the government at that time. I cannot imagine otherwise than that the policy presented by the Hon. Mr. Pickersgill to the House at that time was one that was carefully studied and discussed by the whole cabinet in view of the importance of transportation to Canada. This minister, like other members of the then government, and most of them are still on the treasury benches, must have subscribed to the principles of the act presented at that time.
The people of Canada must also remember and not be beguiled by the minister's frankness, desirable and admi-
March 21, 1974

rable though it may be, that the policy has been administered by a Liberal government since it was introduced. For the past five or six years it has been administered by this government. Finally, they must remember that this minister has been minister of the department for about a year and a half. While it is refreshing and encouraging to find the minister admit the failure of the national transportation policy-encouraging because it at least indicates that a really serious look is being taken at that policy in view of the minister's admission-I just want to say that it is impossible for me and the people of Canada to wash the Liberal government since 1967 clear of any responsibility, (a) for the policy which was a disaster and, (b) for the disastrous implementation of that policy since 1967.
I put this motion on the order paper because the minister informed the House and the country that the full policy is now being discussed within his department. That makes me uneasy. As far as I know, he is surrounded by a good many of the same people who were responsible for the policy introduced in 1966-67. I only hope they have seen the same light the minister has seen, have the same illumination he has evidenced and the same conversion that he has talked about. I hope the discussion inside his department will not be the kind of frustrating effort that I am worried about because, I repeat, many of the same people will be doing it.
Because of that it seemed necessary that this House of Commons discuss this very important subject at the earliest opportunity. Not that we will be able to solve it. My colleagues and I do not claim to have the in-depth knowledge that is necessary to solve every part of this very vexing and complex problem. However, it will give us an opportunity to discuss the general principles which ought to underline a national transportation policy.
I did not have the pleasure of hearing the minister's speech on March 7. However, as I read it, the Minister of Transport suggested there had been no objection to the principle of the bill which forms the basis for the present national transportation policy. I looked up Hansard because I had vague memories about objections voiced by my then leader, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and by myself as a matter of fact. I should like to read from the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on September 2, 1966, as recorded at page 8044 of Hansard just so that the minister knows there were some people in this House who were very strongly opposed to the basic principles that underlay the bill they were putting through and which is now the law of Canada. The hon. member said:
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe that free enterprise and the competitive system of transportation can give Canada an adequate transportation policy at a price we can afford. There may be countries where they can afford to have all sorts of free enterprise and competition; different forms of transportation and different companies competing with each other, duplicating services. However, in a country of 20 million people where, as I said before, we are more dependent than probably any country in the world on getting our goods to market over long distances at competitive prices, where we spend more per capita on transportation than probably any other country in the world, I do not think we can afford the luxury of having a free enterprise, competitive transportation policy.
National Transportation Policy Those are the words of my colleague, the leader of this party on that day. Toward the end of his speech at page 8046 he said these words which seem to me to be relevant:
I am convinced that this government or the government that succeeds it will find that in a few years this transport commission, because of its lack of power and authority, will not be able to solve the problem. If the house does not at this time give that commission some power and put some teeth into the bill, then some subsequent parliament will be compelled to do so, after we have lost valuable years and very large sums of money.
Mr. Speaker, if ever I heard a prophetic statement, in view of the minister's admission of failure, that certainly was one. On January 27, 1967 I participated in the debate on third reading of the bill and said things along similar lines. It was the New Democratic Party which at that time, when the bill was first introduced in Parliament and thrust on the people of Canada, said that a transportation policy based on competition, profit and on the principles of free enterprise would fail. Both my colleague and I emphasized in the speeches, to which I referred that the result of that policy would be great hardships on the prairies, on northern Ontario, on northern Quebec, on the northern part of Canada and on the Atlantic provinces and that it would interfere with the development of secondary industry in all these underdeveloped parts of Canada. We saw that not because we were more intelligent or brighter than other people but because we were not prisoners of the free enterprise fetish that controls the Liberal and Conservative Parties. Because of that we were able to see the consequences of the kind of policy that the Hon. Mr. Pickersgill introduced in this House and pushed through this House. Later, when the policy became law, he was able to leave us and take up the chairmanship of the commission. Ever since Mr. Pickersgill became Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission Canada has suffered without end in the transportation field.
In the time available I want to indicate some general lines which ought to guide us in the development of a transportation policy. I do not expect, although I hope, all my suggestions on behalf of my party will be accepted by all members of this House, but in my view they are basic to any really relevant and effective national transportation policy.
First, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to members of the House and to the minister that we must pass laws, take action and have policies that will make transportation a public utility. A transportation policy for Canada must not be controlled by the principles of profit and by the alleged principles of competition in this society. That does not mean that the transportation system has to lose money. There is no reason for that. The transportation systems have always made money. It does mean, however, that the transportation system in Canada must serve the needs, both national and regional, of the people of this country, sometimes without regard to profit and never governed by the profit motive so far as service is concerned.
I shall have something to say about the Canadian Pacific a little later, but let me deal very briefly with a number of the problems with which the minister is now faced. There is a constant fight against the Crowsnest Pass rates, particularly by the CPR. As I Informed the House in my speech of January 27, 1967 I had occasion over a number of years to act on behalf of some railway unions on a number

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
of occasions. Every time I was in that situation I heard the CPR at that time, through the man who is now president of the CPR, Mr. Ian Sinclair, tell the board and the unions how the CPR was losing money through loading and carrying grain. They used to calculate it into tens of millions of dollars or hundreds of millions of dollars over the years. I remember saying that if they were telling the truth then the CNR and the CPR ought really to be bankrupt instead of being very effective organizations, particularly the Canadian Pacific. The objection to the Crowsnest Pass rates and the calculations they make always are based on comparing the cents per ton mile that they get for carrying grain with the cents per ton mile that they get for carrying those commodities for which they charge much higher rates. That is a pretty false way to tell us they are losing money. That is why I do not accept the statement of the railways, repeated the other day by the minister, that the railways lose money carrying grain.
Sure, they do not make as much money carrying grain as carrying other commodities, but it is their duty to Canada to carry this grain at the Crowsnest Pass rates. Furthermore, when I study the history of the CPR in this country and transportation generally-I have not bothered to look up the details but I have a vivid memory of them-I find that when the agreement for the Crowsnest Pass rates was made with the railways the CPR received additional millions of dollars and additional millions of acres of land as a quid pro quo which enabled this outfit to become one of the largest economic empires in this country. But they forget what they got from the people of Canada and object to the Crowsnest Pass rates. If any one gives in to the CPR on this issue we will have betrayed not only the interests of the farmers in the west but also the interests of all the people of Canada.
The policy which Mr. Pickersgill shoved through parliament in 1967 gave the railways the possibility of entering upon a plan for wholesale rail abandonment. The consequences were disastrous for many communities. Of course, the railways could prove that certain routes, certain bits of line in various parts of Canada were, in themselves, unprofitable. In a country the size of Canada where only 22 million of us are scattered across an entire continent, a relatively smaller population being in the northern regions, of course there are railways lines which are unprofitable and which always will be unprofitable. But that should not be the only reason for permitting a course which not only takes away an essential service from people who deserve it but which has sounded the death knell for many communities.
I honestly sympathize with the minister because of the situation in which he now finds himself. He has to come before parliament, as well as tell the nation on radio and television, to say that there is not enough rolling stock to move all the grain and carry all the other bulk commodities, particularly from the west and from the north, which need to be delivered. And why? Because the railways have decided they can make more money in other ways than by purchasing hopper cars or whatever other cars are needed to serve the Canadian economy. Sir, the railways of this country were created by the people of this country and

they ought, by law, be made to provide adequate rolling stock.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Everybody in this House is aware of the anomalies and discrimination which exists in the freight rate structure. I shall not take any of the relatively short time available to me by citing examples. I am sure that other members of my party, and other members of the House, will do so. But everybody knows how much cheaper it is to ship steers to central Canada than it is to ship processed meat. Everybody knows how much cheaper it is to ship rapeseed rather than rapeseed oil, how much cheaper it is to transport unprocessed raw materials from the north than it is to transport processed goods. This freight rate policy on the part of the railways means they have added another almost insuperable obstacle to the development of secondary industry in precisely those parts of Canada which require it most.
All these difficulties which the minister faces result, as he correctly states, from the fact that competition has never been possible as a basis for national transportation policy. Indeed, profit-making is immoral when applied to national transportation policy in a country such as Canada where transportation, just as much as energy, is the lifeblood of the economy. So my first point is this: we must consider the introduction of a policy which regards transportation as a public utility concerned not with alleged competition but concerned with costs and expenses and with profit only in the sense that it should make enough money to enable it to purchase new equipment and buildings, keep the track in repair, carry out necessary renovations, and so on. All these things cannot be done unless a surplus is earned by the transportation system and no one is suggesting that this should not be a consideration. But the profit objective must be an overall objective for the entire system, not something related to one particular part of the line or to a particular commodity at the expense of the interests of the people of Canada.
We ought not to tolerate a system which denies people a reasonable passenger service. I do not travel by train very often nowadays, but on occasions I do so. I have travelled both on Canadian Pacific and on Canadian National. Neither one is better than the other. The CP is just as bad as the CN and the CN is just as good as the CP. Each is doing everything it can to discourage travellers. If passengers wish to eat on the train in some parts of the country they get a stale sandwich, almost unpalatable and certainly indigestible. The whole atmosphere of the railway cars as well as the service provided is aimed at deliberately discouraging the use of the facilities. What are the railways for? We are making a very grave mistake, it seems to me, because as the minister has indicated, either in one of his answers in this chamber or in a statement made outside the House, developments are presently taking place affecting air travel and other forms of air transport which might well result in rail transportation becoming a great deal more desirable than it has been in the last few years.
I cannot end this part of my comments without expressing my horror at the number of accidents which have occurred on the railways. I expect one of my hon. friends will be dealing with this subject later, if he catches your
March 21, 1974

eye, Mr. Speaker. The CTC has produced a report on this subject. There is no doubt in my mind that one of the reasons for these accidents, and probably the main reason, is the failure of the railways to take proper care of the tracks. This is another way of showing a profit, another way of making money. In this case it is done at the expense of the welfare of Canadians and, sometimes, at the expense of lives.
The second point which the government should keep steadily in mind when considering a national transportation policy is that there must be an integrated national system. We can no longer talk about rail separately, or air transport separately, and so on. There must be an integrated system under which duplication is limited as far as possible, one which recognizes that the so-called competition is a sham. Who is competing with whom? The CN, as well as CP, now controls not only a railway but an air line, shipping, and trucking enterprises. The CP is already in the pipeline business and I gather from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that the CN is also going into pipelines. They are into every form of transport in this country. So who are they competing with, except themselves?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext: And when necessary, they join hands.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Yes. When necessary, they join hands. They agree on rates in many cases. It is meaningless to talk about competition. When one considers the present national transportation policy based on the false concept of profit-making, we realise, to use the words of Pierre Berton, that the national dream has, in this country, become a national nightmare, particularly for the Minister of Transport. And I sympathize with him, though I wish that he and his colleagues who preceded him had shown the wisdom to draw attention a great many years ago to the disastrous effects of the course upon which the government embarked in 1967.
It is in this context we propose that Canadian Pacific Limited be brought under public ownership. When I say this, I am talking not only about the rail operation, I am talking about the whole shebang-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
-the entire economic empire which they built as a result of Canadian grants. Everybody knows the history, and if they don't, they should. Everybody knows about the millions of dollars, the hundreds of millions in grants and subsidies which the Canadian people have given the CP, the millions of acres of land. As a result of these gifts from the Canadian people, CPR not only owns an airline, a shipping line, a trucking line and a telecommunications network, but a large complex in Trail and in other parts of British Columbia, Cominco, the Pine Point mine in the Northwest Territories, other properties all over the country through another subsidiary, and an oil company. Despite the earnings and the profits that these subsidiaries make, every time CPR is questioned about its railway, it says, "You cannot look at profits that we make anywhere else but only at the profits we make from the railway". My answer to Canadian Pacific is that they are making money out of other subsidiaries because the
National Transportation Policy Canadian people enabled them to build a railway, and those profits belong to the people of Canada.
I urge that we bring the CPR under public ownership. I say this not for doctrinaire reasons-though I will doubtless be accused of that-but because of my conviction that it is impossible to develop an integrated national transportation policy and let CPR remain in private hands. If CPR remains a private corporation concerned with making more and more profit, then it will continue in the future, as in the past, to sabotage-I do not use that word lightly but quite deliberately-every attempt to achieve a national transportation policy that seeks to serve the interests of Canada and not the profits of the CPR.
Fourth, I suggest that the government or an agency of the government, whether the CTC or some other body, must have the power to oversee and control investments of transportation companies so as to make sure they get sufficient rolling stock, take sufficient care of their roadbeds, and do all the other things that are necessary to maintain a decent and adequate transportation system.
Fifth, I urge that the government, or an agency of the government, must have real control over freight rates that serve national and regional interests and assist, rather than obstruct, the development of secondary industries in the parts of Canada that require them so badly.
Finally, I urge that the government should appoint immediately a freight controller, not only to meet the immediate emergency in regard to the movement of grain and other bulk commodities, but on a permanent basis to make sure that the railways provide the necessary rolling stock to meet the requirements of our import and export trade and needs of the Canadian people, rather than serve the interests of the CPR, or even the CNR.
There is no doubt that no other country in the world is so dependent on transportation as Canada. This is why we built the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is why we took over bankrupt railways and formed the Canadian National Railways. We realized the importance of a transportation system for the future wellbeing of Canada. The only policy that will serve the interest of Canadians for generations to come is an integrated policy that places all the major transportation systems under public ownership and control, a policy that is governed by those interests, not only national but also regional, that the Canadian people require to be met and fulfilled.

Mr. Speaker, I am well aware that I am not in an easy position, even if the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) made a long statement at first, that I believe to be a very honest one, saying that he agrees with the criticisms I made, but has grave doubts about whether I can follow up on them or revise them.
If I had not made these criticisms, I would obviously be accused of not having made them and of neglecting my duty. Anyway, I think that the rule of the game in Parliament as in court is that you should not try to prove yourself to the witnesses of your opponent. However, I do not hold this against him, because I find that I am not in
736

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
complete disagreement with any of the ideas contained in the resolution of the New Democratic Party.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I find some of these ideas too general. As a matter of fact, the hon. member left himself an opening in his statement, and I believe that he was right to do so. He does not wish to make political gestures which would only be doctrinary and which would refer, if I may say so, to a somewhat outmoded form of intervention by the state.
Indeed, I have heard the same thing said by the British Columbia, the Manitoba and the Saskatchewan premiers. All three make this distinction at all times and I think that they are right. I do not blame them at all.
Of course, we agree on most criticisms. I have made an overall criticism, not to get the attention of the reporters, but to stir up enough attention that those problems might be solved. As we know, some problems are not solved unless the public is mobilized enough to force those in my trade to study them seriously. Otherwise, they are never solved.
And so, I did not do so to attract attention, nor to get into the limelight, Mr. Speaker, but because I think the problem is serious. In my speech, in this House or outside, I did not make a complete analysis of the transport system in Canada. Of course, some things are working very well in the field of transportation. Everything need not be demolished and built up again from scratch. Clearly, when one wants to go from Montreal, or Toronto, to Vancouver the service is excellent. Trains on certain lines are operating quite nicely.
Usually, they operate well when the corporations make profits and on this point I agree with the New Democratic Party. As soon as they incur losses, they are inclined to neglect train repairs, for example, so that means of transport becomes unfit. People are disgusted and do not dare use it.
However, when we consider how subsidies are granted, we realize that we pay, if I am right, some $100 million a year to the railway companies to maintain passenger trains. However, the corporations are not entitled to use one cent of those $100 million to get new equipment. That amount is solely used to cover what are called operating deficits.
Evidently, they are not interested in reinvesting. The cars, the rails are deteriorating and as stated recently, there are even some bridges which fall down and are not rebuilt.
We are therefore in a situation where passenger trains, which are more and more essential to this country, cannot be of any service to the population. Obviously I am accused and we are accused collectively of not thinking since 1967 about redrafting this law. It includes many extremely simple principles and I believe that this has helped solve many problems.
But this left us with large problems on our hands, in other words we thought, and there I do not exclude or excuse myself as indeed the first time in the House, that through competition, between railways, trucks and boats, we would get a near perfect system, which unfortunately

did not happen because in certain areas there is no competition.
You will make your speech in a few minutes, but I am referring to one aspect. Maybe I will agree with you that in certain cases we have not used the powers we have under the law to correct what should have been corrected. In any event, we have a series of problems and all I want to say is that I am not just making a speech after which, having admitted before this House that we have problems, I should just say goodbye. I am being very honest. I think we have already started to solve some of these problems. We have already started negotiations with the western provinces on certain freight rates, and I think we are going to have some concrete results. Maybe we are not going to agree on the conclusions. Okay, that will be part of the political battle which is normal in a country like ours, but at least we are going to have the facts.
The provinces asked for certain cost disclosures and they are going to get them. The committee to study those cost disclosures has already started to work and we hope it will be successful. We have included branch lines, and that is something we think is very positive. The problem now is in respect of what we are going to do when the lines will no longer be frozen. This is a good question, but do not ask it because I am not in a position to answer it at this moment.

Mr. Speaker, I will then try to give my speech a style which is somewhat higher than the heaviness attributed by others to bring it down. In any case, I wish to speak of transportation problems. There was also the development of the north. To my mind, the department has some very interesting accomplishments to its credit. I refer here to airports and highways. We are undertaking a study to determine the possibility of building a railroad to serve the Northwest Territories. Substantial efforts have therefore been made. There has been progress in the field of winter navigation.
If we compare, which is perhaps a normal and a very tempting thing to do for a government in power, if we compare our system with that of other countries, the United States, France, Germany or Italy, I am sure that we have to conclude that ours is the best. However, the best system is not the same as a perfect system nor is it a system that cannot be improved upon. It is indeed possible to improve it considerably.
March 21, 1974

We are making efforts in the area of freight rates. I think that considerable efforts have been made in the area of northern development. In the area of civil aviation, we are also making concerted efforts to obtain the share of the market we are entitled to. These are facts, Mr. Speaker, and this is why I should not like anybody, including myself, to give the impression that everything that has been done up to now has been useless, that this was a case of misdirection and that all civil servants were wrong at the same time. This is not true. A mistake was made, and I agree with hon. members of the New Democratic Party when they say it was wrong to believe that the profit principle and competition would settle all problems. Well, there are large areas in our country where it will never be profitable for a railway, bus or truck company to operate and make money. It will never go there. This is the very principle on which private enterprise is based, and I do not see anyone in this House, not even among the NDP members, who would accept to open a highway or establish a bus service in the great north if he had to absorb a one or two million deficit every year.
The structure of our system does not allow it but, as a country, we must serve the people living in these areas, and it is there the system proves its inefficiency, that is the nature of our whole country has not been taken into account. However, I must mention that serious efforts have been made, that we have the parts of a system that works extremely well. The problem before us now is to correct the defects. Of course our friends in the New Democratic Party remid us of nationalization. And some find it a panacea to nationalize CP, non only CP, but all it subsidiaries, which means a great deal of people. I think that the CP company has 47 subsidiaries, if I am well informed, and it administers hundreds of millions of dollars.
Some may suggest that these subsidiaries were born from things given to them by the Canadian people. This is a public and political debate that would be extremely interesting to have one of these days, and maybe our views do not differ greatly on this matter. However, should CP now be brought under public ownership? I would rather see a policy and national objectives set up first in order that we may know exactly where we are going, and see if that is necessary. Personnally, I am not interested in bringing CP under public ownership. Mr. Speaker, if hon. members want to know how many companies are involved in the field of transportation in Canada, I have figures here-21,000 in the trucking industry and 48 in the rail transport industry because CN and CP are not the only ones operating a railway. BCR was also brought under public ownership in British Columbia but several companies do not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. There are 694 air carriers. With respect to gas pipelining 175 companies are involved in that field. I admit quite frankly that before stomaching all that, Mr. Speaker, I would much rather see an adequate policy set up because if we had to deal with all that tomorrow morning I really wonder how we could manage to do it. I think we would not be the only government to react that way and if our hon. friends opposite were on this side of the House they would think it over twice before passing such a general resolution although I do not object to it in principle. It seems basic to me for a country like ours to
National Transportation Policy have control mechanisms and if at some point private enterprise is not doing what it should we should have the means available to us to make it act as it should which is often something we do not have.

Those are our major objectives. We now have the problem of the lack of railway equipment and cars. It is always the same situation. The government says to the railway companies: Listen, you must be motivated by profit, your grants will be reduced; you had better try to compete with trucking and so everything will be for the best in the best of worlds. But when those companies consider they are making no money by investing in cars they do not build any. To me the problem is as follows: Should we chance buying equipment which next year, for instance, will not be used because the year will not be as good as we thought, or should we have a situation where we would have an extraordinary year but where we will not be able to haul our merchandise for lack of the required equipment? Decisions must be taken. Who takes them? Private companies, of course. Naturally we could ask CN to build cars but CP can see no reasons to build cars unless the level of our economy becomes higher than they forecast or than we forecast.
Mr. Speaker, we are also at grips with the whole problem of urban transportation. As I said once, I do not know where, everybody believed a few years ago that rail transportation was obsolete and that air and road transportation were the modes of transport of the future. Billions of dollars were invested in highway and airport systems. Today, all urbanized modern societies realize more and more that they made a mistake, and that they should never have abandoned railways as a means to link our urban centres. For instance, it is possible today to have a train that runs at 200 miles an hour. I am sure that you will travel by train between Ottawa and Quebec City and that it will be faster than by plane or by any other means of transportation. Therefore, we must re-assess our traditional concept. We are not the only ones who made this mistake. All European countries did the same. There used to be streetcars in the cities. Today people think that it might be better to have streetcars, less pollution and fewer cars parked along the streets.

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
That is the policy that the federal government must develop. We must do it, not on our own, but with the co-operation of provinces and municipalities. Recently, Mr. Speaker, I accepted in this House the suggestion that a controller be appointed, somebody who might report to us on how railway cars are allocated in Canada. I prefer this idea to the suggestion that somebody be appointed to decide, because I wonder to whom this person would report. Would he report to a politician, to the Minister of Transport, who would decide?
We could say to the CNR that it has enough cars in British Columbia and that it should send the cars to the east. Surely, we can solve the problem within the structure. However, we should know what it is so that if there is something wrong in the system we can use this information and all the facilities of the government to correct what must be corrected. But, I am not sure the best formula would be to give this power to a controller. As a matter of fact, the only exception I take to the resolution is the reference to the general nationalization of the CPR and its subsidiaries. I do not take this position merely because it is a matter of principle with me but because I do not believe it would be useful to do that. I do not know. If some people believe that the CPR has stolen from us and that it owes money to the Canadian society, let us settle that with the CPR and tell it that this money belongs to the government of Canada and not to the CPR. But let us not mix that with a national transportation policy because I think the two are quite different.
But if it should be necessary to nationalize the CPR in order to have a really integrated system, if it should be silly to have two railbeds following the same path and the CPR should not want to correct that situation or wish to sell their property at such prices that they become prohibitive when they know they got it practically free, then we can use the instruments we have and I would have no objection to nationalization. So I think this is the situation. I do not say no immediately. I just say that the first thing we have to elaborate is a new policy, a corrected or improved policy, to determine national objectives and after that see by what weapons we can really attain those objectives. Whatever some people may think I have no vested interest anywhere. If the party to which I belong should have a vested interest to the point that it would not be acting in the interest of the public just because some of them were linked a little too tight, well at that time you know I think I am free enough to say just what I think about the whole business.

But up until now, I think what we have been doing has been proper. We have been trying to develop the north. We have been spending a great deal of money in opening up the northern part of British Columbia. I hope we will be successful. We are trying to see if we can build some railway cars, including hopper cars. We are making a real effort in that direction. We are trying to correct the situation in the west and the situation in the maritimes. We are trying to see, in co-

operation with the province of Ontario, for example, if it is possible to have good commuter trains like those, for instance, between Richmond and Toronto and Barrie and Toronto.
We have a similar proposal in respect of Montreal and probably will receive proposals in respect of Winnipeg and Vancouver. This is what we are trying to do. We are trying to find new ideas so that the needs of the people will be met, not only their needs but also their expectations. I am reminded of something, and I see one of my colleagues here who is interested in that. Many years ago the CPR decided to abandon the small train from Montreal to the north country. In French there is a song about this, "Le petit train du Nord". Perhaps from an economic point of view it was a very expensive link to the north. However, the highway is so crowded that the people no longer can move and they ask why the train is not reinstated or why they cannot have a fast train to Montreal. I would be ready to do the same thing any place there is congestion because we know in this country of ours we have too many cars in the city which are causing pollution. One of the solutions is trains, and this is what we are going to do. Mr. Speaker, I think I have exhausted my 30 minutes. I thank you very much. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has put on another virtuoso performance in the course of his speech, but I feel we are still somewhat in the dark in respect of what he intends to do. It is a tribute to his extraordinary personal qualities, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) said, that he makes the sort of disclosures he does with frankness and honesty as he did on March 7 in this House and today. Nonetheless the implications of what he said, though well received, are staggering and disturbing to all Canadians.
The current Speech from the Throne indicates that the government has attached great importance to transportation as related to regional development. Now, it is apparent that not only are we without the capacity and capability to solve many of the urgent problems relating to transportation, but we are also left with the very foundations of our regional development policies in jeopardy. I was surprised that the leader of the NDP did not touch on this point.
It is said very unequivocally in the Speech from the Throne that:
Transportation in particular is a key factor in regional development.
Canadians are now told the unpleasant truth that two of the very high priority items necessary for the country's economic progress are in jeopardy. I say in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that if the government is at all capable of embarrassment it must indeed be very embarrassed today. I challenge members to name policies of greater importance to our national economic well-being and progress than those which are necessary in these two vital areas of transport and regional development. And yet, by the admission of one of the key ministers in the government, we are given the hard facts of life as to how deficient we are in these vital policy areas.
March 21, 1974

Our national transportation problems hold back our economic development in all parts of the nation. They are impeding our capacity to move commodities. They are injuring our trade relations with other nations. They are hurting our economy in so many ways that it would take hours to detail the damage done by the government's lack of policies. I am sure all of us remember that not long ago, when we were debating the so-called energy crisis, it was pointed out, and seemed to be tacitly accepted by the government, that we did not necessarily have an energy crisis, but that if there was an energy crisis at that time it was related to transportation because we did not have the capacity to move fuel from areas of surplus to areas in need. It was not that we did not have the fuel, it was that we lacked the capacity to move it.
I am sure the Minister of Transport must have realized at that point, and perhaps for the first time, just how much work had to be done to solve our transportation difficulties. I may say that I am very happy that the minister at this point does not agree with the NDP that we should exclude the private sector from transportation. If the NDP could say with any justification to the House that those Crown corporations which we have in the transportation field are manifestly superior to those which remain in the private sector, that they are cheaper and more efficient, then I suggest with some logic that they could put forward this type of motion for debate today. As I say, I am happy that the minister does not agree that this is a proper policy for him to consider, although of course he has left the door somewhat open.
I bring to the attention of the minister, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has done in the past, and presumably will again in the future, that motor transport is one of the policy areas in which the government has been most deficient. As a suggestion from this party, Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister to consider, in conjunction with the provinces because as he pointed out the provinces are, of course, necessary partners, some sort of practical policy to establish an interprovincial trucking board, or to establish reciprocal arrangements, so that the barriers and the impediments confronting Canada's motor transport industry can be removed. This must be one of the key factors in considering a transportation policy for the nation.
It is nearly impossible to pick a particular aspect of transportation that is not in difficulty, whether it be labour relations, administrative efficiency, or policy goals. Our national Crown transportation agencies and companies are in trouble. The minister himself is certainly well liked, well respected, and well qualified in labour relations and trade union affairs. I can think of few people in this House, if any, who are better qualified in this respect, and he should be especially qualified to cope with and solve the problems that exist in this particular aspect of transportation. I am speaking of labour-management difficulties, and I am thinking in particular of Air Canada.
But if one can believe what the minister is saying-I am sure we all want to do that-what he is saying publicly, what he is saying on the radio, and is reported in the press as saying, that unless he can get better co-operation and control he will resign, then surely it must be because he is not getting the proper type of co-operation from his cabi-
National Transportation Policy net colleagues in expediting the kind of decisive legislative and administrative changes needed to cope with the very complex difficulties he has to face.
Certainly nothing has changed since his predecessor said two years ago, I believe it was on March 20, 1972:
I propose to bring before the House in the next session three important pieces of legislation on which work is proceeding at the present time. The first of those is a bill designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, thus divorcing it, as it were, from the CNR. I will also introduce a Canadian National Railways revision act and a companion piece of legislation covering amendments to the Railway Act. Hon. members will know how involved and far-reaching these changes are; they have been asking for them for the last two or three years. These changes have entailed a great deal of work, which is still proceeding. I believe, however, that these bills are essential and I will bring them forward as soon as they are ready.
Obviously, those bills were not ready before the House was dissolved and an election took place. However, the real point is that the country has been under the administration of a Liberal government for about ten years. The minister is no recent recruit, such as I am. He has been here for a good many of those years. He has been associated with the cabinet, and with affairs of state on a high level. While it is very admirable that he has been so honest and frank with us, nonetheless it is a great indictment against the administration that now we are faced with the revelations recently made to us concerning our present transport policies and how they affect the economy of the country.
While the minister is undoubtedly correct in seeking the co-operation of the unions in an attempt to overcome the lack of efficiency in our transportation systems, I think he should be more concerned with management. I submit that it is here that many of the problems have arisen. In my opinion management has been derelict in adapting to technological changes, and has shown great deficiencies in labour and public relations, as well as a lamentable lack of foresight in adapting to changing economic conditions. Certainly the minister, as I have said, is uniquely equipped to deal with labour relations and he has competent colleagues to assist him, such as the former minister of manpower and immigration and the former minister of labour, the latter having an enviable record in such matters.
I would strongly urge the minister to study seriously the question of encouraging discussions between labour and management, under the auspices of the Department of Labour, with the idea in mind of having the labour contracts for our two major railway systems expire at different times. I realize there are reasons why this might not be acceptable, but on the other hand it could help avoid nationwide paralysis in times of labour disputes, paralysis which because of its magnitude hinders normal labour-management relations and causes parliament to step in, perhaps not always when it is in the best interests of the workers. This type of arrangement is normal in other industries such as the automotive industry, where one big company sets the trend for the others. As I say, I realize there may be objections. Perhaps some labour people think this is not a good idea, but I urge the minister, as part of his on-going policy re-assessment, to consider it.
It would also be a good idea, and I make this suggestion to the minister at the same time although it should more properly be discussed in connection with marine transport

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
policies, to press on with establishing separate Crown corporations to manage the ferry services operating between our mainland and the maritime provinces. They, too, are affected when an incident arises where our national railway system and the CPR go out on strike. This is something that the minister should take under advisement, and I hope he will.
As far as direction from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is concerned, with respect, Mr. Speaker, I doubt if he could run a church bazaar. I do not think he is a practical type of person and I doubt whether the Minister of Transport will get very much assistance or direction from him. Surely, that is not the case with the minister himself and some of his colleagues, however. I think he will agree that at this time we do not want to exclude the private sector from this nation's transportation systems. I am not surprised to see the NDP indicate this sort of action in this motion. It is consistent with the principles of socialism and while we in the Progressive Conservative Party cannot agree with them, still, we would like to be able to respect the sincerity of our friends to the left.
Many Canadians know how difficult it is to believe in the current New Democratic Party philosophy because even their own followers realize that they are not sincere and have lost credibility as an opposition party without having the intestinal fortitude, on the other hand, to form an open coalition with those on the treasury benches. It must be, to put it in Biblical phraseology "sharper than a serpent's tooth" for the leader of the New Democratic Party to read in the Vancouver Sun of March 2 that one of the candidates nominated by the federal NDP, Ken Nova-kowski has dropped his candidacy because, as reported in the article:
The federal party caucus has compromised too much, . ..
They've backed some pretty wish-washy legislation ...
The principles of the NDP are more important than gaining or losing a few seats.
They have some principles, apparently, in the eyes of their supporters outside this House but their credibility in this chamber has diminished. It is interesting for us in the official opposition to watch and listen to what my friends on the left say about transportation, and other things as well. They may explain and rationalize all they like. They want the credit for anything constructive this parliament has done, but they accept none of the blame or criticism.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party, a prominent lawyer, has come up with a new legal or parliamentary concept-it could be termed "responsibility without guilt". He castigates the government for its many failures in transportation and other fields but the only time he sounds sincere is when he attacks the official opposition. His logic must be, "the government is not doing anything so let's attack the opposition and blame it on them". He does not include himself in this particular category of an opposition member, obviously.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Progressive Conservative Party realize that the problems of transportation are immense, but much can be done by determined effort and some sort of pragmatic, down to earth approach; doing something that needs to be done. I believe that the majority of

members of this House sympathize with the minister when he says that he does not appear to have enough authority to make the type of managerial and policy decisions that he seems to think are now necessary.
We advocate the immediate reassessment of the current goals and managerial policies of Air Canada. We feel that the object should be to ensure that these Crown corporations are devoting sufficient energy to their principal role of providing efficient transportation of goods and people in this country and that they cease participating in activities which are only incidental to this role. There is a great need that the primary role of transportation in this country be filled, and these agencies should be devoting their energies to this end.
I should like to make a suggestion to this House, although it is not primarily related to what I have already said. As far as the safety aspects of transportation are concerned, I believe that the minister should give careful consideration to making public the findings of accident investigations carried out by the CTC, by his ministry and other investigative bodies. The secrecy that presently exists is consistent with the attitude that I find so aggravating so far as the management of our Crown corporation is concerned.
It is obvious that the Minister of Transport is not able to exert sufficient control over the Crown corporation and private sectors in transportation. Certainly, as hon. members from all parties have pointed out, there is a basis for authority to be exercised under the National Transportation Act and, as pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) yesterday, under the Railway Act. If the minister is sincere in wanting still more authority to deal with these problems, I am sure he would get it speedily if he were to bring forward some concrete measure that would demonstrate his desire to take effective action.
The fact that members have been so reluctant to pass the CNR financing bill, is related to the attitude of which I have just spoken. This particular bill, now known as Bill C-5, previously known as C-164 and before that C-4, has a ridiculous and almost farcical history. It is an indictment of the way these Crown corporations are managed. If you look at the history of this matter, it is easy to see why members of parliament get their backs up about the way the government handled this aspect of the financing of Crown corporations. Little wonder the government is having difficulty getting that particular bill passed.
The executive officers of Air Canada and the CNR will not divulge how much their many vice-presidents are being paid or what their specific responsibilities and duties are. Although I was promised at the last committee hearings by Air Canada that they would let me know how much rent they paid last year, I still have not received the information. The whole financing setup of CNR and Air Canada should be changed, and I put that suggestion forward to the government through you, Mr. Speaker.
In effect, we now have a period covering the CNR and Air Canada financing from January 1, 1971 to June 30, 1974. The very fact that this is possible demonstrates how little control this parliament has over this aspect of Crown corporations. It is obvious that the financial affairs of CNR and Air Canada are not really in the hands of the
March 21, 1974

elected representatives any more. I say to my friends on my left, why nationalize all Canada's transportation if the government cannot control our present Crown transportation agency?

speechtext:
That may well be.
I should like to deal with marine policies now, Mr. Speaker, which are of particular interest to me, coming as I do from eastern Canada. It is well known that these are vital to Canada. We have one of the longest coastlines of any country in the world and a great deal of interest has been expressed in reviving a Canadian shipping fleet. This nation should share in the transportation of its export and imports. About one-third of our imports and about 40 per cent of our exports are moved by water. Canadian vessels, chiefly in the Great Lakes fleet, carry about one quarter of our water borne imports. The remainder is carried in foreign flag vessels. That is not a healthy condition. Canadian dollars-$133 million in 1969, for example - were drained away to pay freight charges to those vessels. Much of that money could be kept at home if a Canadian ocean fleet were available to carry our exports and imports.
At the beginning of the 1970's Canada had begun to conclude long-term contracts for large-scale export sales of products such as iron ore, coal and wheat. The prediction is that exports of this type will grow steadily throughout the 1980's. Many will go to the Orient. There is no reason at all why Canadian flag vessels should not carry these exports.
We, in this party, believe that we should definitely concentrate on establishing a viable Canadian merchant fleet. We should also upgrade the Canadian Coastguard service, to provide more comprehensive and efficient environmental and fisheries surveillance and protection. That definitely is needed. I also urge the minister, and I hope he will consider my suggestion worthwhile, to establish an Arctic fleet capable of providing economic transportation to northern Canada and establishing more firmly Canadian sovereignty in northern waters. I also suggest that the minister should pay more attention to the needs of the Ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert, because of their potential for reducing costs to western Canadian shippers.
I see that you are about to say my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. May I close by suggesting this to the minister. If he will bring forward constructive legislative changes which are essential for any reassessment of this country's transportation policy, 1 am sure he will be able to count not only on our support but on the support of the majority of the members of this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member of the Creditiste Party who was to speak just now for allowing me to participate ahead of him. I have a train to meet and I appreciate his co-operation and hope to reciprocate one day.
For the moment I want to talk about two subjects. Neither is controversial and both fall within the ambit of
National Transportation Policy government responsibility rather than of private industry. Both the situations, to which I am about to refer can be rectified. I do not intend to talk at great length, because I know that some people have talked on one subject for years and will talk on it again. I am glad to see the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) in the House as he, too, is interested in the question of pensions of retired railway workers.
I do not pretend to be an expert on the subject of pensions. There is an organization or association which is now looking after the pension problem. It calls itself the Senior Council of Canadian National Pensioners Association. It is headed by a close friend of mine from my community, Dick Wooraker. He gives nearly all his spare time, working virtually without pay in the cause of retired workers.
Several private members bills have been presented on the subject. The one which has intrigued me most is Bill C-139, proposed by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) which, if passed, would go a long way towards rectifying the problem of retired workers. The hon. member might be fortunate in having his bill adopted in private members hour, because it involves nothing more than a change in the regulations.
The group in which I am particularly interested and of which the hon. member for Moncton is aware is a group known as ICR workers who draw their pensions from what is known as the provident fund, that being a fund set up by Parliament away back. Some said it was a wonderful plan. I remember that when my dad died at the age of 56 he was receiving $58 a month pension after 41 years of continuous service, including service in the war years. I always remember the last cheque arriving a few days after he died and our having to send it back. The plan provided nothing for the survivors, for the wives and children. Only a few thousand workers are involved. The union must bear some of the blame for what has happened, because it showed very little interest in that particular group which, for one reason or another, was left with little in the way of pension. That is, when the workers reached age 65, they had little in the way of pension.
I want to talk about other subjects, as well. Let me say that the provident fund was set up by an act of Parliament. It is true that, in 1935, the people involved in that plan were given the opportunity to join the CNR plan. In those days many people were unemployed and those who were not did not have the money to join the CNR plan, the result being that only 110 out of 3,000 elected to transfer to the CNR plan. On the second opportunity in 1941 only 86 transferred to the CNR plan. As of January, 50 employees still worked for the railway and belonged to the old ICR provident fund plan. I understand that about 2,000 pensioners right now are drawing money from the fund.

speechtext:
I must confess that I have forgotten to mention the subject before, but I am happy to see the hon. member for Moncton present. I know he is concerned about this, as he and other members of the House have talked about it privately on many occasions. I hope they take up the cudgels on behalf of those people who draw benefits from the provident fund.
My other point, and I am trying to stay within the 15-minute limit, concerns transportation, particularly transportation by water in this country. A situation has been developing in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec, which in time I suspect will affect Saint John and Halifax. For years, as those who know anything about longshoremen will tell you, men who worked on the waterfront did casual work which needed strength and little else. In the old days when a ship came in the employers went out to hire men to unload that ship. A battle of wits developed. Workers wanted to stretch out the only work that might be available that week for as long as possible, and ship owners wanted cargoes to be unloaded as quickly as possible. You ran into the strange circumstance on the waterfront of workers impeding productivity and employers engaging in a degree of corruption in order to speed up production.
The situation has improved as a result of the work of the National Harbours Board. Many of the corrupt practices of the past have been virtually eliminated in the trade, in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. Good collective agreements have been entered into, under which virtually every impedence to productivity on the waterfront has been eliminated. In return for the elimination of restrictive practices, the employers, in the collective agreement, have agreed to guarantee the workers 37 weeks of work per year at 40 hours per week. We talk about unemployment insurance; but what is it? It is a plan of which employers have taken advantage. The workers have assumed what should be the social, moral and legal obligation of employers, namely, improving the conditions of workers, by providing income for workers all year round instead of for three, four or five months of the year. We generally forget that the UIC helps employers as well as employees. The ones who cry most about it are the biggest users of the funds, the employers in the construction industry, and yet unemployment insurance benefits subsidize their payroll.
In these three ports we have employers who brought in a modified guaranteed annual income. They said to the workers, the longshoremen, eliminate the restrictive practices in the existing collective agreement, the size of the gang, give us complete flexibility and in return we promise you work for 40 hours a week for 37 weeks over the life of the contract, that is the normal period in the ports because of ice.
What has happened has been that, as a result of this better collective agreement, we have a tremendous increase in productivity in these ports. Add to this

increased productivity in these ports, increased mechanization of what is known as break-bulk cargo; add to that the tremendous growth in the containerized field or technological change, as was mentioned by the very eloquent member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). When you put those ingredients together, you have a situation in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec which results in greater volume with substantially less people to the point that management, some months ago, bought up, if I may use that expression, 550 men. In other words, 550 men were fired or laid off in return for a certain amount of money. Despite that, there is still a surplus of men available on the waterfront.
When that collective agreement comes to an end at the end of this year, unless something drastic is done, it is very obvious what is going to happen. Management is going to refuse to continue the feature of a guaranteed annual income for the duration of the new contract. They are going to try and reduce the work force by between 500 and 1,000 men. It is quite natural that the longshoremen will want to revert to their old practices, if only to protect the only job they are trained for or capable of doing.
What has management done to alleviate the present dilemma? Management bought up these men at $12,000 each. This is being paid for by a royalty assessed on the goods coming into the port. That is fair enough. The money is to be borrowed from the bank. If it is to be repaid in a very short period of time over the life of the present collective agreement, it is obvious that the royalty has to be fairly substantial since the money involved is fairly substantial. If this is done, the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec will no longer be competitive with New York and other ports.
X am not a member of the cabinet. One or two of the cabinet members present are not paying too much attention anyway. If they were, they would appreciate one thing. That is, all that is needed to make the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec competitive with New York, Saint John, Halifax, Boston or any other port around the world, is in place, productivity, containerization, and mechanization. Incidentally, buying hopper cars for private industry is never a problem. Why then is it a problem for the government to act as a guarantor and nothing more in order that the needed bank loan can be amortized over 10 or 20 years. The employers are capable of paying the money back over any period, but in order to pay it over the life of a contract, the royalty must be of such dimension that the port would no longer be competitive. This problem has been unsettled for six or seven months. Nobody really knows where they are going.
You can say what you like about the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), but he is a humanitarian. He understands the most important thing is people. I am encouraged that he is there. If anyone can solve the problem, he can. The minister understands human relations. He understands that productivity is based not only on machinery, but on the willingness of people to accept it. What he needs is the support of the rest of the cabinet-
