speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 4 of this year, in this House, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I asked for the unanimous consent of the House so that ways would be found to reduce the number of railway accidents across Canada, especially derailments. I even proposed the appointment of a royal commission on the administration of railways and on the means to be taken to remedy the consequences of this deplorable deterioration of this service of prime necessity and national interest.
As usual, my motion under Standing Order 43 did not receive the unanimous consent of the House. I notice with pleasure today that a full day has been reserved for the study of the desired improvement in railway management.
In my constituency, at Mont-Joli, a Canadian National employee in charge of checking the trains retired last
27398-48S

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
December. He was not replaced. By the way, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that I sent him a request about this and that I have not yet received an answer in my office. I asked him to be good enough to appoint an immediate replacement for this supervisor who had retired.
Afterwards, 24 cars left the rails at Routhierville, approximately 70 miles from Mont-Joli.
Another time, a freight car crashed into the Mont-Joli station partly demolishing it in a tragic and funny way. Mr. Speaker, it should not be forgotten that the Mont-Joli station is especially busy since Price Brothers operate a sawmill six miles from Mont-Joli and ship all their lumber by CN railway. It greatly increases the activity in the Mont-Joli railway yard.
As I said, the Price Company uses that railway yard so that the railway traffic controller plays a vital role and cannot vanish with impunity. In early March, there was another funny and costly accident which could also have been tragic. Seven or eight passenger cars ran off the line near Luceville between Mont-Joli and Rimouski. That time, the engine as well as eight cars completely left the tracks. Luckily, there was no loss of life, but I think that some people were injured. It should be noted that 15 minutes before the derailment of the east-bound train another passenger train had just gone by.
I should like to make a suggestion to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) about the supervision of railway tracks. I would suggest that after the passage of every train, the track be inspected in order that such accidents may be prevented. This would provide employment, since people complain about the high rate of unemployment today. At the same time, it would prevent costly accidents like those that have already happened.
Early in March, another funny and costly accident happened, as I mentioned earlier, when a car lost its shipment of $27,000 between Toronto and Winnipeg. This shipment consisted of 5 cent coins which were sown over a land unsuitable for cultivating silver or nickel.
I agree that those are trivial incidents compared with the big businesses that handle billions of dollars right across Canada, one of the wealthiest and most capitalistic countries in the world.
I think we should congratulate the opposition party that took the initiative of calling the attention of the government to our railroads which have long been the pride of Canadians, financiers, administrators and employees. One wonders now whether that reputation is not about to wane.
As I cannot trust my impressions alone in forming an opinion, I get my information wherever I can, but always from the most reliable sources. For instance, early in January, a CP report published in Le Droit of Ottawa mentioned that it is the CTC that asks the companies to reduce the speed of the trains, to limit their loads and better inspect the rails, and this all year round.
They try everywhere to reduce the number of employees, thus increasing unemployment and encouraging lower quality services. There is nothing to laugh

about, Mr. Speaker, when we look at all the derailments which have occurred since 1970. Referring to statistics for 1959, I find that 40 derailments occurred that year, 69 in 1969 and 132 in 1972, accounting for an average increase of 90 per cent in those three years.
That makes me suggest that railways are in a very bad shape. I was listening earlier to the minister expressing his intention to improve that situation.
In the past, as I remember, the ballast under the rails rested on slag and accidents were fairly infrequent because the tracks were very well maintained. There were four mem assigned to the maintenance of each seven mile section. Inspections took place daily and often after the passage of various passenger or freight trains.
Today it is thought wise to extend sections to 18 or 20 miles, I think, and two employees and one foreman look after and maintain the tracks.
With regards to the inspection of railways, I wish to inform the minister that, it is rather funny to say, the employees and the inspectors of the tracks now travel often by car on the highway. They drive around and claim that they did inspect the tracks.
Also, I would bring the attention of the minister to the fact it is often said by public servants that there are more chiefs than Indians, and to my mind such is the situation prevailing now in the CN. There are too many civil servants and not enough employees to maintain and accelerate the development of railways.
I do not know if the minister is aware of this, but there are civil servants in the railways companies who enjoy all sorts of privileges, including the use of a company car, credit cards, paid expenses and often a bottle of scotch, up to a maximum of $50 a month.
When they need to replace a window at the Rimouski station, they must send for a worker from Campbellton to do the necessary work.
There is so much merchandise, pieces of rail and sleepers along the way between Halifax and Vancouver that, if an inventory were made, the amount would be enough to pay the salaries of all employees for a year.
Therefore, the CN is certainly poorly administered. There are too many civil servants, too many unjustified expenses and an enormous waste of money.
If we compare the derailments that took place during the same period for CP and CN trains, we find that for 1969 to 1971 CPR had 52 derailments and 80 in 1972. When compared with 132 for the CP, one must admit that a private company certainly takes more care of its rolling stock and railway tracks than a publicly owned company such as the CN.
I called for a royal inquiry on the quality of railroad transportation on October 24, 1973 in a speech I delivered in this House. Members of the New Democratic Party go faster and recommend definite measures, such as, for instance, public ownership of the CP and integration of the whole railroad transportation system into a single government controlled utility.
March 21, 1974

That is what I call coming quickly to extreme and definite solutions before reconsidering the whole problem and comparing the efficiency of both systems, namely a national enterprise on one hand and a private enterprise on the other. Therefore, we should analyse all comparative results of both companies, namely the CNR, a government controlled company, and the CPR, a privately owned company.
That is the main point to be clearled up. Despite its profits that are distributed among its shareholders, one often wonders whether the private enterprise is not even more efficient, more profitable and less expensive than a public enterprise. A serious royal inquiry might enable us to determine more precisely the deficiencies of the present administrations and to take remedial action as required without disturbing anything in the existing financial and administrative structures.
It is important, Mr. Speaker, to know how to distinguish between casual and localised deficiencies of administration that may be corrected right away, and basic and structural deficiencies that would demand a major overhaul and a complete change in organisations. Under current circumstances, what is the best decision to take? Should we take a drastic decision prior to a royal inquiry or should we conduct a royal inquiry prior to taking a decision fitting the circumstances?
I do not think this question will be settled today but I commend the NDP party for drawing the attention of the government and of this House on a major question which deserves our best attention and efforts if we want to maintain our railways prestige and current reputation which are recognized throughout the world as most efficient in such a great country whose needs and temperatures are so varied.
Today is not the day to deal with the many circumstances connected with the administration of our railways but the whole financial system of the CN and CP needs an in-depth study. In both cases, we are speaking of financing in terms of billions and in both cases an interest rate differential of 3, 5 and 10 per cent has considerable effects on administration costs both for the state company and the private company.
And the whole question of interest rates, in the field of railways as in other areas, is a matter under the supreme authority of the government of Canada under the British North America Act. It is not because of the dividends paid to CN stockholders that administration is too costly but because of the interests paid on its debt in the form of bonds and, in this connection, the CPR and CNR are both suffering from exorbitant interest rates on billions of eternal debts which are renewed automatically every 20, 30 or 40 years at higher interest rates. The same applies to the bonds issued by the government of Canada.
Perhaps you noticed again that last Monday all our major newspapers mentioned that the government of Canada is floating a $550 million issue at 6'/2 and 8 per cent, of which $350 million will be used to redeem a maturing issue which was marketed at 5 per cent. Is it known that without any further effort on their part, Canadian and foreign millionnaires will receive some $15,000 or $30,000 more per million in the future, that is a total of $65,000, $70,000 or $80,000 instead of $50,000 during
National Transportation Policy several years more, and that finally, the government, unable to pay for its debts, will have to renew its loans at still higher rates? Is that known? Was that thought of? Are these mere trifles? Certainly not, Mr. Speaker. The CN should go through a good inventory so that measures can be taken to ensure the best decisions are made to meet more satisfactorily the needs and hopes of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by my leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), contains a fundamental part of the New Democratic Party's policy on transportation. I am sorry that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has had to leave, but I hope that his parliamentary secretary will hear my words and take them back to him, and that they will persuade him to accept the points made by my leader as well as the points I have to make.
This issue has been raised two or three times in every session of parliament in the past almost six years that I have been here. The same problem has confronted us in almost every one of these debates; it is with us now, and it will continue to be with us unless we make some fundamental changes in transportation policy and in how we operate our transportation systems.
Transportation is fundamental to the social and economic life of Canada. It is so essential to our national wellbeing that it falls naturally into the category of being a utility. The priority of any utility, of course, must be the provision of service. The principle of service must replace that of competition and must supersede that of profitmaking. As my leader said, this is not necessarily socialist dogma, though socialist thinkers originated the idea. It has been accepted by governments and parties of all political stripes that anything that is an essential public service is best operated as a utility that is publicly owned and operated.
Society, after many decades of bitter experience, has learned that competition and private profit have no place-and I repeat, no place-in developing and operating an essential public service. Society has brought into being many kinds of services under public ownership, such as our streets, sidewalks, highways, sewer and water systems, city transit systems, and in much of Canada our telephone and electrical systems. Major national modes of transportation remain under a mix of private and public ownership, the prime objective of both of which, I regret to say, is competition and profitmaking.
The present national transportation policy and the legislation of 1967 enshrine withim them the principle of competition, which does not allow for or require the meeting of the transportation needs of the people or the economy. Neither do they recognize transportation as a vehicle to foster regional economic development. For too long our transportation systems have discriminated against people and places because of our geography. Those same systems were also party to the prevention of economic development in Atlantic and western Canada.
The New Democratic Party believes that these major modes of transportation must be placed under public democratic ownership and made to function for the real social and economic use of this country. By making our

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
major transportation systems a public utility, so-called competition is then automatically ruled out, as has been the case over the years with other kinds of utilities. That is the first essential of a national transportation policy which will bring about a real national transportation system, namely that it is a publicly owned, operated and controlled utility.
To be more specific, the New Democratic Party believes, and a New Democratic Party government would undertake to implement, the following. I shall go through my list of points for as long as my time will permit.
First, to emphasize what my leader had to say on this point, and again I hope what I have to say will persuade my hon. friends in other parties, we would bring into public ownership the Canadian Pacific system, now called Canadian Pacific Limited. This would include the subsidiary companies over which Canadian Pacific has ownership or control and which are felt necessary either to the wellbeing of a national transportation system or other national interests, with the full proviso that no employee shall suffer from the transfer to public ownership. For example, in addition to CP Rail right of way, trackage, buildings, rolling stock, etc., all lands and mineral rights still held would be returned to the people of Canada. I might say that while the figure of 25 million acres is the one recalled by the public and members here, they should know that all land grants to the Canadian Pacific system since 1881 from national, provincial and municipal governments total 43,962,546 acres. These lands and the mineral rights must be returned to the people of Canada.
The taking into public ownership would include CP Air as that is an essential public utility of transportation. It is foolish to have competing airlines. It would be as foolish to have competing subway systems or sewage and water systems. Competition has no place in a national public utility. Something that is a natural monopoly should not be the subject of competition.
CP Oil and Gas and Pan-Canadian Petroleums, both Canadian Pacific subsidiaries, should, in the national interest rather than just transportation interests, be taken over. I believe they would be marvellous addition to a real national petroleum corporation, and, as the government is proposing legislation in that area, this would be a good beginning.
CP hotels are essential and a proper adjunct to a publicly owned and held national transportation system. CP Telecommunications should also be publicly owned since, for the purpose of market sharing and the elimination of competition, this area is already jointly operated with Canadian National and they have divided up the country between them, so that all that remains to be done is the transfer of ownership. CP trucks and ships again represent a necessary part of a national transportation utility system. CP ships could provide the beginning of a real Canadian merchant marine.
My next point is that the Canadian National Railway system must be relieved of the burden of debt that has been continually compounded since its inception as a way of bailing out bankrupt private railways. One of the methods I suggest of doing this is by having full disclosure in

respect of those who hold the remaining private debt of the CNR and transferring that private debt, which I believe amounts to something in the neighbourhood of $1.8 billion, to the public accounts of Canada, and in this way the people of Canada would finally become the sole shareholders of their railway.
In addition, our national transportation policy would requires the elimination of freight and passenger rate inequities through equalization or subsidization or a combination of both. There should be a moratorium on rail line abandonments with an assurance that the railways maintain adequate standards of facilities and services, as well as maintaining sufficient rolling stock and locomotive power.
In addition, the NDP advocates the restoration of certain services already eliminated. May I say to all of those who think that all we should do is take over the railway right of way and road leeds, this would be an economic disaster, since both railways have allowed a major portion of their trackage and roadbeds to deteriorate to such an extent it would require the expenditure of several hundreds of millions of dollars to bring them back up to proper standards, and the taxpayers of Canada would again have to pay for the mistakes of previous transportation policies and the deliberate mistakes, at least in my mind, of our railway systems.
My next point is that by direct assistance or in conjunction with the provinces we should develop a publicly owned, provincial and regional air carrier system which would be integrated and operated in conjunction with our national air transportation system. We should have provision for substantial expansion of air services, routes and facilities at subsidized fares and rates in the northern territories and probably in the northern parts of some of our provinces.
My next point is that our policy would provide that a rate-setting structure, developed under a public utility approach, would be based on the cost of shipment rather than on the value of the commodity shipped. An NDP federal government, acting in concert with provinces and territories, would assume direct responsibility for all matters of transportation rate setting and related activities rather than allowing federal regulatory bodies to assume wide discretionary powers in this area. In order to reflect regional concerns in the operating of a public transportation utility there should be direct regional representation on regulatory bodies responsible for transportation policies, and the provinces would be fully involved in the setting of trucking rates across the country.
My next point is that the Port of Churchill must be developed as a major supply depot for the north and, along with Prince Rupert, be expanded to handle larger quantities of western agricultural and finished products. In other words, an NDP government would develop these into major seaports.
The next point I have here is that we would provide for greater participation and input by transportation employees regarding their pensions, working conditions and safety procedures. Beyond that, we would give them more direct participation in the operating of the railroad or the airline because they know how to run the transportation systems by which they are now employed.
March 21, 1974

The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) spoke out partially against the idea of public ownership in this field. I have only to remind him and all other members that with the exception of Canada and the United States, the governments of pretty well every other country in the world, of all political affiliations and persuasion, democratic and dictatorial, have transportation systems which are publicly owned and operated. We can learn some lessons from these countries, and I think of nations in western Europe, Japan, Australia, the Soviet Union and Scandinavian countries, all of which gave up a long time ago the idea of transportation being a place for competition or profit making.
I want to submit, as sincerely as I can, that there are some areas of human endeavour in which those two principles, which are adhered to by those who claim to believe so strongly in the so-called free enterprise system, have no legitimate place, and where competition in fact prevents such an endeavour from functioning properly. Even the Minister of Transport now admits that competition in transportation in Canada does not work.
With a publicly owned national transportation system, with all major modes of transportation included, we could have the efficient and integrated transportation of goods, services and people at the least possible cost, without discriminating against Canadians because of where they happen to live, meeting the transportation needs of any given part of the country, and meeting the transportation requirements of the producers of any given goods whether they be agricultural or manufactured products. It would allow for a much more equitable division and distribution of Canada's processing, manufacturing and distribution industries. Most of all I believe it would help to do as much or more for national unity than anything else.
One issue which has divided Canadians for decades has been the kind of transportation and communication systems we have had. This has caused us to quarrel among one another since the 1880's. This is still the case. The bitterness and division, I submit, would be substantially reduced if this and succeeding parliaments would move to bring about a publicly-owned and operated national transportation utility in the best interests of Canadians and the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the motion before us I am sure no one will disagree about the problems referred to in this motion connected with the transportation system. I think there is agreement that there must be more integration in respect of certain forms of transportation and that some immediate action must be taken to speed up the movement of grain and other important commodities across this land. I believe also there would be general agreement to the appointment of a railway transportation controller or coordinator immediately. However, I believe the agreement ends there.
We have before us a simplistic socialist policy, based on the philosophy, that civil servants can provide an effective and efficient transportation system better than the private sector. That I suggest is rather naive. It is the major thrust of the NDP solution, but that is the kind of unadulterated
National Transportation Policy socialistic rhetoric in which they engage. I was interested to note that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) indicated some qualified support for the proposals advanced by the NDP. I am not surprised, given the cosy relationship that exists between the NDP and the Liberals. I would suspect the government could very well be directed on that course. Judging from statements made by the minister outside the House, this particular course may be undertaken sooner than later. There has been a great deal of cross fertilization between the two groups.
One thing my NDP friends forget is the fact that there are two major nationalized transportation companies in this country which do absolutely no better and in many cases worse than those involved in the private sector. If nationalized transportation is the most desirable thing, the CN should be a model of railway transportation services in this country. I ask hon. members opposite and their colleagues to the left if, for example, the CN does any better than the CPR in the movement of grain, in the movement of lumber or in the movement of fruits and vegetables, either east or west, or does the CNR maintain its trackage and its equipment in a more desirable fashion than the CPR. The answer to that is no. The NDP know this very well and yet they say we should nationalize everything. This does not add up. The point I wish to make very emphatically-and here I point out that the CNR is as guilty as the CPR-is that the railways have failed to fulfil their mandate to the Canadian people.
The mandate of the railways is to provide an efficient and effective service of rail, freight and passenger transportation for the Canadian people. Furthermore, this government has failed to hold the railways to this mandate. The government does have power to do this. I intend to point this out later in my remarks. Let us look at the operations of the CNR. Year in and year out the government-owned corporation is heavily subsidized at the expense of the taxpayers. Rather than have a model of an advanced futuristic rail system, we have an antiquated system that has failed to recognize and develop new technology. It has failed to upgrade and maintain its equipment. It has failed to maintain its trackage in a safe and efficient condition. It has failed to meet the challenge of the twentieth century in respect of rail transportation requirements.
What has it engaged in? My hon. friend from Central Nova pointed this out. It has engaged in some exotic collateral ventures such as building towers, establishing shopping centres, and engaging in other real estate ventures such as luxury hotels. Only the CN can lose money in the operation of the hotels. It has even been involved in consulting agencies. I want to reiterate that the government must tell the railway to honour their commitment to the Canadian people and do the job for which they were given the mandate.
I believe the prominence of the railroads must be restored. They are a vital asset of this country. They must be upgraded, conserved and fully utilized. But the Liberals, and this particular government as well as previous Liberal governments, have allowed the railways to merrily go on their way. This has cost the taxpayers a great deal of money. The CNR now has a debt of $1.8 billion with notes bearing 5 per cent interest. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
private corporation can borrow money at that rate of interest. Still the CNR loses $25 million a year. And this is a company which has assets totalling $4 billion. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) can squawk all he wants. He will certainly have an opportunity to speak later and I will listen to him, although I have listened for many years and never heard him say anything constructive.
Let us not forget-and this is for the benefit of my NDP friends-that back in 1952 the government wrote off half of the CNR debt of $1.5 billion and further reduced it by $120 million later on. That is the fabulous success story of the CNR. I do not think we have to blame its failure on competition but rather on mismanagement and government misdirection.
What is the CNR's major competition? Of course, it is the trucking industry. The CNR was losing money long before the trucking industry was established and long before the National Transportation Act was in effect, so I suggest the argument proposed by the NDP has absolutely no validity. Using their argument we could say we would be better off with one political party rather than four. We are down to three now. I do not want this to be taken as a vendetta against the employees working for the CNR because there are many faithful, hard-working citizens of the country employed by the CNR. However, I do have some criticism of the management and above all the concept of nationalized enterprises.
What about the trucking industry? I want to reiterate that so far as I am concerned, in my humble opinion the principle of competition is not all that bad in fostering an effective transportation network. Certainly there have to be trade-offs when considering competition and the necessary economies of scale, but on the whole I suggest it has been a reasonable and realistic goal. However, the government has failed to implement the provisions of the National Transportation Act to carry out the basic principle of that legislation, namely, competition. It has failed to take the necessary initiatives. I blame provincial governments as well, including my own province of Alberta, for failing to reach any sort of uniform agreement so far as reciprocal arrangements and a uniform code of regulations are concerned so that the trucking industry could operate throughout this country unimpaired and uninhibited. If the provinces cannot reach some agreement, the federal government should take stern action to bring about an agreement that will allow motor vehicle transport to operate effectively across the country. At one time the federal government had that power, but the Liberals gave it away back in 1954.
Just look at the melange of weight restrictions that the motor trucker is faced with across the country. For example, look at weight limits for a tandem tractor-trailer combination. In Manitoba we have a GVW of 80,000 pounds, in Saskatchewan it is 74,000 pounds, in Alberta
72,000	pounds, in British Columbia 82,000 pounds and in both Ontario and Quebec it is 82,000 pounds. The western provinces seem to be the ones that are squawking the loudest about the removal of freight rate anomalies. Perhaps they should be the ones to take the initiative in building up their road systems, in conjunction with the
[Mr. Mazankowski.l
federal government if necessary, so that a uniform weight code can be established.
Another matter which is greatly bothering the trucking industry at present is the status of the railway freight rate freeze. In short, this has cast a very gloomy shadow upon the trucking industry. We all know that freezing railway freight rates automatically freezes the trucking industry's freight rates because the two forms of transportation compete with each other. Yet we have the government granting something like $41 million to the railways to compensate them for the losses they incurred as a result of the freeze, while nothing goes to the trucking industry. In the miscellaneous estimates committee today we were not even given an opportunity to ask for an explanation of that situation. Mr. Speaker, we have three major railroads operating in Canada today. We have the CNR, the CPR, and the "railroading" job that is done by the miscellaneous estimates committee.
The government does absolutely nothing for the truckers. The trucking industry may very well be wrecked if something is not done soon. As I say, if you freeze railway freight rates you automatically freeze trucking rates. The trucking industry is not immune from inflationary pressures. Diesel fuel has risen by six cents a gallon since July last, and I understand it is due to increase in the order of 8 cents during the next month or so. Salaries to employees have increased by 15 per cent. The cost of tires has increased by 15 per cent to 20 per cent, and parts by 20 per cent to 25 per cent-if they can be obtained. How is this industry going to survive? Is the way it is being treated fair? I say it is discriminatory.
Let me warn the minister and his socialist friends that truckers have been instrumental in holding down freight rates in Canada. Moreover, they have been instrumental in making railways toe the line in maintaining decent services where competition exists. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Transport alluded to this at the western economic opportunities conference in Calgary when he said that competition between the railways and the truckers, as was envisaged by the National Transportation Act, has been of great benefit to the people at large. I agree with that. I only hope he will give equal treatment to both sectors of the transportation industry. As a matter of fact, he himself said we must recognize the importance of equal treatment for all modes of transportation. I would ask the minister to live up to that undertaking, because if the trucking industry disappears or is greatly diluted we all know what the railways do when they do not have competition: they simply charge what the traffic will bear. I suggest to the minister, in all fairness and on behalf of the truckers, that if he is going to subsidize the railways he must give equal treatment to the truckers.
I have mentioned the record of the CNR as a Crown corporation. I could also refer to Air Canada and its move into collateral ventures. Air Canada is part of the same family as the CNR and therefore has the same lofty ideals. My colleague from Central Nova touched on those. We are getting into a situation where these Crown corporations are engaging in far too many other activities rather than fulfilling the mandates which they were given. This is why we propose to separate the operations of these two Crown corporations and appoint different boards of direc-
March 21, 1974

tors which would make them answerable and responsible to parliament for meeting their particular obligations. We firmly believe that under the present system, corporations such as Air Canada and the CNR do not answer effectively to parliament. We have lost parliamentary control.
We have had relatively poor performance from Air Canada, particularly in the areas of service and profit, notwithstanding the fact that it has had basically a captive market, low interest on its debt, an excellent route structure, the highest load factor in the industry and behind it the nationalistic pride and sentiment which make Canadians travel by Air Canada. In short, it does a poor job when compared with other trunk carriers on the North American continent which do not have these built-in advantages. This Crown corporation to which we have taken strong objection basically has become a haven for political friends of the government, immune from the shareholders, immune from the close scrutiny of parliament and engaged in the pleasant task of empire building. We all know what happened in Air Canada with respect to labour relations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the motion moved by the leader of the NDP because it gives me an opportunity to deal with a subject that it is very much in the minds of Canadians, including those in my constituency. I shall deal mainly with that part of the motion which reads:
-as a public utility to serve Canada's transportation needs instead of being governed by considerations of competition and profit-

This is just the occasion I had been waiting for to reassess in fact the purpose the Canadian railways had assigned themselves. The original purpose and the philosophy that prevailed when the railways were built were to forge a link between all Canadians from all parts of Canada. It was somewhat like the spirit that prevailed at the time the CBC, Canada's national network, was developed-a venture or a project that could not be expected to record a profit in the foreseeable years and that the state alone could provide that service to which all Canadians were entitled. Railways belong to that type of service, Mr. Speaker. That service should be available to all Canadians. As the years went by, Mr. Speaker, I believe the purpose for which the national railways were built was lost in that under the banner of effective administration we are more interested in profits and in showing interesting figures to shareholders than in serving the purpose that the railways had first undertaken to achieve.
If one looks at the circumstances in which railways were built, and we were reminded a while ago that no less than 43,920,000 acres of Canadian land were given to the two main railways companies, one realizes, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose in building those two railways was really to provide communications between all Canadians, somewhat, as I said a while ago, like the spirit that prevailed when the CBC was established. That philosophy is waning because of that passion for administrative efficiency that calls for showing profits.
National Transportation Policy
I believe the time has come and this motion is the opportunity we need to reexamine perhaps the real purpose of the railway companies.
We must consider the enormous costs of transportation at the present time, when 36 per cent of the mileage travelled by the public in urban centres such as Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Hamilton and Quebec City, is done by automobile. Actually, while the cost of transportation by car continues to increase and that this mode of transportation is very costly for governments, we do not have at our disposal the figures concerning the costs of maintenance and construction of roads in the province of Quebec.
As a simple example, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that, recently, either last October or November, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) announced the participation of the Canadian government in the development of autoroute No. 13 which will join Mirabel Airport to Dorval Airport. Thus, for a road of 13 linear miles, the cost is estimated at $130 million, or $10 million per linear mile.
I wonder whether the Canadian economy can afford such a fabulous luxury at $10 million a mile. I would recall the huge amounts which have been invested at the beginning of the 20th century for building tracks such as those I have in my constituency. This is a CPR track between Montreal and Mont-Laurier and it is used by only three trains each week at hours which do not meet requirements. I intend to revert to this subject which is of some interest to my constituents.
However, I would like to proceed with my examination of transportation cost in Canada, specifically the most popular means of transportation-cars. Transportation expenses are becoming increasingly prohibitive for Canadians and both CP and CN are studying this continuously aggravating problem to try and find solutions.
In the Speech from the Throne there are several important items but two of them are particularly important for those interested in transportation problems.
Let me read extracts from the Speech from the Throne, and I quote:
Transportation in particular is a key factor in regional development. A number of measures will be taken in the larger context of ensuring that Canada's transportation capability supports the government's national goals and is safe and efficient.
And further on:
Steps will be taken to end any discrimination in freight rates.
Another part in the Speech from the Throne advocated and I quote:
Improvements in Canadian grain rail transportation capabilities.
Certainly the government is most concerned about this question in view of the cost of road building and of the necessity to protect the environment, a question increasingly exciting to Canadians. The Department of Transport is already engaged in important research work, Mr. Speaker, to develop means of transportation meeting present needs.
I indicated a moment ago the concern of my constituents for the transportation problem. I thank the Minister of

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
Transport for mentioning in his speech my interest in improvements to transportation in my constituency. It becomes increasingly expensive to build highways, bridges and overpasses. A rational use of structures built some eighty years ago must be done. To this end, Mr. Speaker, I have made representations to the president of the CPR to re-establish the services of this company to travellers between Montreal and Mont-Laurier, a run which goes through a good part of the constituency I represent in the House of Commons.
To my first letter of December 21, 1973, the president of CPR answered in somewhat unusual terms. This is what he answered to the request I made, and I quote:
In its decision and order of December 14, 1973, the railway transport committee of the Railway Transport Commission declared the present passenger service to Mont Laurier uneconomic and ordered that the service be continued.

As I indicated a while ago, Mr. Speaker, I know the operation of the railroads is to become profitable in the name of an efficient administration, but I say that it is a challenge to the administrators of the Canadian Pacific; and I say to them that if they gave adequate service, with modern equipment, I am convinced that in next to no time the service we ask of them would be profitable.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that since I launched that campaign of representations to the CP administration, no fewer than about twenty municipalities in my riding have already supported them through resolutions. In fact, 14 associations made representations and recommendations to me, assuring me of their support; a large number of citizens in my riding who travel daily between Montreal, Sainte-Agathe, Sainte-Adele and Saint-Jerome have written to me expressing their support for the campaign I launched with the view to restoring the Canadian Pacific service.

To this end, in my last letter to the chairman of the CPR on March 4 I made the following recommendations:
1.	Immediate inauguration of daily commuter service between Mont Laurier and Montreal with trains leaving Mont Laurier every morning and returning each evening.
2.	Beginning in the fall of this year, regular weekend ski trains providing same-day service to the Laurentians and back to Montreal.
That is for the skiers who go to the Laurentians region.
3.	Renovation of existing stations along the line as required.
4.	A survey of the potential commuter market between St.-Jerome and Montreal. (One is reminded of the recent order of the Canadian Transport Commission that the CNR provide commuter service between Barrie and Toronto).
5.	An in-depth assessment of present rolling stock which is used to service this line with a mind to providing whatever equipment required to fulfil future needs. (The practice of allowing usage to meet the service that existing equipment can provide is "putting the cart before the horse").
6.	A study to determine the linking of present rail commuter needs with a future rapid transit link between Mirabel airport and downtown Montreal. It appears that for much of the route, existing CPR lines will be used.
(Mr. Dupras.l

Those, Mr. Speaker, were my representations to the president of the Canadian Pacific and I hope that he will give them serious consideration because I have no intention of changing my mind in view of the unexpected support that I am getting from the population of my constituency as well as of Montreal, and in view of the ecological needs that are at stake. I now find it unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that each time the construction of a new road is announced, a swath of at least 200 feet of often fertile land is taken over and the scenery is irreparably damaged.
For all these reasons, I believe that the facilities that the CP owns from Montreal to Mont-Laurier should be put to use as soon as possible.
I therefore ask all those who are concerned with this question to support me because I believe that this line which I mentioned earlier could show a profit in a few months, and that it could enable us to prove that the Canadian population really needs a modern public transportation service. If we compare the services and equipment that the Europeans have with our own, it is easy to see why Canadians no longer travel by train.
This is regrettable because it is an excellent way to travel, and a safe way which does not endanger the environment.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover of this motion, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), for his initiative, and as I stated at the beginning of my comments, he has my support for one part of the motion, that which concerns the railway operations of the Canadian Pacific.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the time remaining before six o'clock I shall try to cover a number of items. I know I will not complete my remarks before six, so I shall probably speak again at eight o'clock.
I was interested to hear the minister's remarks. In his speech, when speaking about the difference between the Tories and the Liberals, he said the only difference was that the Liberals are more skilful. I am sure he did not mean they are more skilful in bringing forward a transportation policy, because that is what this debate is about. Members of my party for years have been saying there is no difference between the Liberals and the Tories. I was pleased to hear such a distinguished gentleman as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) confirm our view.
Others taking part in this debate have dealt with various difficulties associated with achieving an efficient and integrated transportation system in Canada. They have also talked about how competition in the private sector has impeded the functioning of an industry so necessary to our economic survival. Some of us in my party view transportation not only as another industry but as a required public utility.
The leader of my party asserted that we face our present transportation mess because both our multinational corporations, the CN being the so-called public corporation and Canadian Pacific being the private one, have followed
March 21, 1974

identical policies directed to making profits which are largely based on the principle of greed. I wish to spend a few moments talking about the philosophy of greed and what greed does to the morale of those working in the industry. I say that because a high level of employee morale is vital for the successful running of any transport system. You can have all the good equipment in the world, but if the morale of the employees is poor you will not get the most out of your equipment. Productivity will lag, no matter how much you have spent in purchasing and maintaining equipment.
I will make a few general remarks on topics such as wages and working conditions and, of course, rail safety. Then I want to speak briefly about the inadequacies of pensions, especially with regard to those who have already retired and have nobody left to speak on their behalf except possibly the muscular member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In all these areas the record of the railway companies has been appalling.
At one time, most people who worked for the railways looked on railroading as a lifetime career. Now, because of conditions which have persisted over the past 10 or 20 years, that attitude on the part of employees has been eroded to the point where they are leaving the railways in droves. The CNR, with respect to which information is more readily available and which is therefore subject to more criticism than is the CNR, loses 15 per cent of its work force every year. This year, probably about 7,000 employees will leave.
Let me tell the House that 23 per cent of the CNR work force has been on the job less than two years. How can such a proportion of new people, no matter how skilful, be as efficient as older, more experienced workers? How can they know as much about rail safety, for instance, as workers who form part of a more experienced work force? It seems to me that such factors add to the inefficiency of the system. This holds true no matter what your policy may be or how progressive and enlightened it is.
How can tracks, equipment or anything else be maintained when 20 per cent of the machinists, 18 per cent of the electricians, 10 per cent of the carmen and at least 40 experienced yardmen left the railroad in disgust in the Vancouver area in 1973? You would need to do a lot of looking to find another national industry in which such a high proportion of workers is leaving. Where else will you find such a rot in the work force? If you add the scores of truckers who left after difficult wage negotiations, and add the fact that wage negotiations are so lengthy, so protracted, the fact that the companies know parliament will bail them out, and they will not bargain in good faith, and the feeling of railroaders working on the job that their views and suggestions count for nothing, you will not wonder why the trains do not run on time.
Last week two Kamloops men were killed in a tragic CP derailment at Spences Bridge in the Fraser canyon of British Columbia. The very next day there was another derailment near the same spot. In case one thinks such derailments are rare, let me put the record straight. I have a number of figures relating to these derailments. They are current; that is to say, up to date. My only difficulty is that I cannot find them. If we could call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I could use the dinner hour to find these figures.
National Transportation Policy The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger): It is six o'clock in any event. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the recess at six o'clock I was saying that the two tragic deaths in the Fraser Canyon last weekend were part of a pattern. I was about to cite some figures to support my contention. I received these figures from the Canadian Transport Commission today: they list the derailments and accidents on railway lines between Vancouver and Kamloops from January 1, 1953, to March 1, 1974, a period of 21 years. In the case of Canadian National derailments, there were 86 accidents, 9 killed and 41 injured. For other accidents, and I presume these had to do with unmarked crossings and automobile accidents, there were 10 accidents, 1 killed and 23 injured.
The CP rail record is equally appalling. There were 29 accidents, 5 killed and 10 injured. For other accidents, and
1	again presume this to be rail crossing accidents involving personnel other than railroaders, there were 19 accidents,
2	killed and 19 injured.
I think I have given sufficient documentation and statistical material to indicate to members present this evening that this particular piece of trackage is a suicide run as far as Canadian railwaying is concerned. There has been a good deal of carnage throughout the Fraser canyon for a great number of years. I make no reference whatsoever, except incidentally, to the number of people killed building the railway. I think we have to admit it is the toughest terrain in the world. In spite of the fact it is difficult terrain, we have to assure ourselves that the maximum safety standards are always adhered to.
According to an editorial in the January-February Canadian Railwayman, the number of CP and CN derailments across Canada in 1972 is up three times over 1959 and nearly double that of 1969. The CTC became so alarmed over this increase that a rail safety committee began an intensive study of the problem in 1970 and to date had issued three volumes of a five-volume report. If the last two are anything like the first three, they will be equally devastating in their criticism of current safety measures on Canadian rail lines. Canadian Railway Labour Association spokesman J. M. Walter, in the same editorial, places the blame for wrecks squarely on the shoulders of the rail companies. He asks why, if as they railways insist many of the committee's recommendations have already been instituted, the derailment record remains so bad, and why there was not a cutback by at least two-thirds in 1973 over 1972.
There is no doubt about it, without pressure from CTC reports and the safety advisory committee the rail lines would have persisted in ignoring safety and men's lives would have been sacrificed for the sake of the buck. In the northern part of British Columbia, track maintenance is

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
deplorable. Last fall, in seven subdivisions with authorized manpower calling for 126 section men and foremen, only 56, or less than one half, were on the job. I had an opportunity to ask Mr. McMillan and his chief of operations, Mr. Hunter, about this in committee hearings. He admitted that even the new rates of arbitrated pay were still too low to attract sufficient manpower to that region.
We could go on to document the fact of poor track maintenance and resulting poor rail safety because it applies throughout the whole system, but perhaps I have made the point. Men on the job and retired railroaders constantly write me with complaints and suggestions. Members of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers have been under a legal threat since 1972 because they dared to push to CPR with respect to a litany of 30 or more and working condition safety complaints, many of them centering in the Fraser caynon.
After last weekend's accident, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications received a wire from the engineers calling for the installation of ditch lights, slide fences, padded engine cabins and roll bars to prevent future fatalities of the kind that occurred. I have a few suggestions to offer the Canadian Transport Commission in their pursuit of better safety. First, I think we have studied this problem long enough. We should start telling the railways what to do, give them a time to improve and, if they do not improve, take strong sanctions against them. Second, we should start publishing the results of inquiries, produce the facts, name names and shed the full light of publicity on the people responsible for the problem. There are far too many rail accident inquiries hidden in CTC files. If the CTC needs a PR man or a PR department to publicize what they are doing, then I urge them to obtain one.
Third, the present regulation limiting a railway employee called before management on a disciplinary matter regarding one of his colleagues to speak on his behalf, is not sufficient. Why not consider making a CTC official available for all kangaroo courts in which they issue demerits, and make certain there is an independent person in addition to the employee concerned and the management personnel, before management is allowed to hand out demerits. There is a club in Vancouver called the Take 30 Club. This is a group of people who have had to accept at least 30 demerits. It puts them in a certain kind of jeopardy.
Fourth, the CTC should constantly and actively seek information from the rank and file, and not limit itself to receiving information from labour representatives who have to pay part of the national rail leadership in Ottawa. Someone has suggested that with the publication of reports from the CTC rail safety committee and the stab-lishment of the CTC union-management safety advisory committee, things are improving. We are rounding the bend, they say; there is light at the end of the tunnel. Let us hope that rounding the bend doesn't lead to another derailment, and that the light at the end of the tunnel is not affixed to the front end of an on-rushing freight train.
I should not like to turn my attention to a matter of great importance, that is, the subject of pensions, especial-

ly those of retired railway employees who have no one to fight on their behalf, neither the unions nor railway management. One is reminded of the plight of the family of the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) whose father was a railwayman. I do not think he would mind if I were to reveal the story.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) when addressing the House earlier today talked about the enormous land grants given to the Canadian Pacific in the eighties and nineties. Those grants were made 75,80, nearly 100 years ago. Yet they are still called up continually by detractors of this railroad. Let us think about the background to these land grants. In the eighties everything possible was done to attract settlers to Canada. One way of doing this was to give land to a corporation and hope that the corporation, on a private basis, could stimulate settlement.
The CPR did a great many things for this country. The program put out by the CBC based on a story prepared by Pierre Berton is the story of the building of Canada. Looking back now, it might seem the country was well rewarded in return for these grants of land. The railway encountered extraordinary difficulties when it tried to raise money by pledging what were then considered to be worthless land holdings. The government gave the railway a few built-up lines, $25 million and a pile of land, and that is all the company ever received.
What do we hear from socialists on this side of the House such as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre? He wants to take over the CPR. He wants to do that because it is the only railway we have which has made a profit and made it consistently, and done a job and done it consistently. The hon. member's party is only calling for nationalization of this railroad because party dogma demands it, because of a philosophy developed in Regina years ago in another era. These people to my left simply carry it on because they have no new policy, no new philosophy, no new drive for the development of Canada. They do not believe in the building of Canada. They believe in the nationalization of Canada. They believe in putting Canada in blue jeans. They believe in making everybody equally poor. They do not really believe in the development of a transportation system.
A week ago I was amazed to read in Toronto papers and elsewhere statements made by the minister that the transportation system is botched up. Well, who has been botching it up? I was a Liberal government which appointed the famous Edgar Benson to be in charge of the CTC. It took a guy who had messed up the financial affairs of this country and put him in charge of transportation so he could mess that up, too. I pity the minister if he has to work with Edgar. But he should have known better when he accepted this portfolio.
The minister says he has no authority to do things. He has all sorts of authority under the National Transportation Act. It is time he used that authority to develop a
March 21, 1974

consistent transportation policy. A new transportation policy does not need to be based on the nationalization of the CPR. That is old crap. If we are talking about the nationalization of railway companies, let us compare the activities of the CP and the CNR. On one hand we have a railway which from rail operations alone was able to make $57 million a year, according to the last financial statement; on the other hand we have a railway which before debt is taken into account makes $23 million and, when debt is taken into account, lost $17 million.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
They talk about debt. When I was a student in high school they said the reason the CN failed to make a profit was that it was forced to carry a heavy load of debt caused by being obliged to take over a lot of bankrupt railway companies. The truth is that the debt charges, in terms of total revenue, borne by the Canadian Pacific is in excess of cost of interest on debt paid by the Canadian National. Yet every year this House is required to pour money into the CNR to keep in operation the inept management of that railroad.
One of the major problems the country faces is this: we are stuck with a national railroad which is improperly and ineptly managed. It is not managed as a business; it is managed in a political fashion, and therein lies the problem. It is not managed sensibly or capably. In the early 1950s, the financing of the CNR was reorganized. We settled all its debts. It was virtually debt-free. Who was appointed to manage that railroad? A pseudo-politician by the name of Donald Gordon. He had a great record of experience: he had worked for the wartime prices and trade board; he was in charge of the Bank of Canada. This gave him long experience in working for government. They put him in charge of CNR. That is how government departments run government departments.
How is Air Canada run? We appointed a president, a fellow by the name of Baldwin. He worked for the Department of Transport for a long time and then suddenly it was decided he should go into the private enterprise system and run Air Canada. You know, Mr. Speaker, you cannot run a business like you run a government department because politics and business do not necessarily mix. Business is concerned in doing things effectively and efficiently, while politics is not business-oriented. Politics is interested in social affairs, and those two things do not mix.

One of the difficulties about Crown corporations is that in the railway field the CPR has it made. I am sure friends to my left will agree when I say that the CPR is responsible for moving 55 per cent of the grain in this country while the CN is responsible for moving 45 per cent. The CPR doesn't like to move grain any more than the CNR does, but the CPR is really smart; they hide under the umbrella of state ownership and they move exactly 55 per
National Transportation Policy cent of the grain. They organize their boxcar movement on the basis of the efficiency of the CNR. If the CNR were to move its quota of boxcars, the CPR would move its quota of boxcars. The CPR is fortunate to have the CNR around because the CNR, a nationally-owned corporation, is the prime example of poor, inept socialist management of a Crown corporation. This is exactly the kind of thing that happens when you have socialism-you have inept management, which leads to inept political management.
If, Mr. Speaker, you had had the opportunity to attend the meetings last fall of the House committee on transport and communications when it was debating Bill C-164, you would have been shocked at the way the management of the CNR and Air Canada spent day after day trying to bamboozle members of parliament. We asked them some embarrassing questions, like some of the questions I asked about the Bessborough Hotel. Let me tell the House about the Bessborough Hotel scandal. This is a hotel which is worth, on the books, $3 million to $4 million. If appraised on the basis of efficient management, it is only supposed to be worth $800,000. The Bessborough Hotel property occupies some of the choicest land in the city of Saskatoon. The bricks and mortar alone, on anybody's appraisal, are worth $1,600,000.
Somewhere along the line the CNR lost $400,000 in 1971 and another $400,000 in 1972. That year they decided they had better fix the place up, so they spent another $214,000. So there is $1 million. They then decided they would like to get rid of this lemon because they could not operate it properly, so they called for bids. A fellow went from Saskatoon to Montreal and offered $1,600,000 for the hotel. They snapped that up like a lunge going after a small fish. Having bought the hotel for $1,600,000, it was immediately mortgaged for $2 million. That is the kind of management you get from socialism. They do not know which end is up, and if they do know which end is up, they do not know where down is.
The Hotel Bessborough scandal-which is what it is-is what you get from the management of Crown corporations. One reason we get that kind of management is that politicians appoint to boards of directors people who really have no vested interest in the success of their company. They know that if they need a little more money to do the job, they can always call upon the government. They plead with the House that they are doing a necessary job, just as the CNR pleads with the committee for $5.6 million for hotel expansion because hotels are necessary for the community. Yet the CNR has not yet invested 1 per cent of its own money in hotels.
The history of Crown corporations in this country has been abysmal. The suggestion of the New Democratic Party that the railroads be nationalized is amazing. They suggest the CPR be taken over by the government. At least at the present time the government of Canada is collecting enormous corporate taxes from the CPR. What kind of corporate taxes is the government collecting from the CNR? None.
The truth of the matter is that a railroad never makes a profit. And if it did, it could go on to the year 3000 and never pay a dime in taxes. The truth is that this railroad

National Transportation Policy
must continue to be fed and fed because it has management that is inept. The reason its management is inept is that the government uses jobs on the board of directors of the railroad, and this, that, and the other thing which goes with the perks of office, as a reward to its friends. It looks after those people it likes to look after.
The problem with Crown corporations is politics. This is why the socialists want to become involved-because they are in league with the bureacrats. They really do not care about the ordinary guy, about the taxpayer, and neither does the government. They want to reward their friends, to look after everybody. They have a paper image, if I may call it that. This is the kind of situation we have with socialism, and that is the intent behind this motion.
Of course we have many transportation problems in this country, but a lot of them are caused by stupid, band-aid measures that are taken by the government. For example, we have a frozen branch lines policy. Although there are rail lines in this country that are no longer required, we do not have a government that is prepared to do something about them.

I should like to repeat what the minister stated: we do have some transportation messes, and in some areas competition is not working in the way that all parties in the House thought it would back in 1967. This is one of the main reasons the Ministry of Transport was restructured in 1970, so that the minister could be given a total overview-I repeat that-of what was required on a modal and intermodal basis with the basic aim of making transportation in Canada more responsive to the objectives of the government and the needs of the people.
At that time the government said that as new social and economic demands evolved, adjustments would have to be made in the years ahead in the areas of administration and regulation. This is a continuing process and never will it be resolved by a one-time decision of any government. The process is working. The very fact that we are discussing transportation today as an important issue is proof of that, Mr. Speaker.
I think we all have a common objective, and that is an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest cost. That principle, incidentally, is already contained in the National Transportation Act. What this government is striving for now is the mechanism which will ensure that we can achieve those objectives in the short and long term. Unless it is absolutely necessary, it is not this government's desire to operate transportation systems, but rather, as I have mentioned before, to ensure that adequate systems are in place and
March 21, 1974

operating efficiently for the people and the economy of this country.
As the minister mentioned this afternoon, we have 694 commercial air carriers in this country. Many people do not realize that fact. We also have 48 railways which are regulated by federal and provincial governments, and we have more than 21,000 trucking companies. In addition to that, of course, we have pipelines, ferries, urban transportation systems and terminals. I do not think any government would want to be the operator of all those facilities. However, by and large most of these systems are dependent upon one another and this is why we have been evolving the Ministry of Transport concept over the past four years. The operative word is "management" and not "operation".
The minister mentioned this before, but I believe it is worth repeating: there are real problems within the area of transportation. Sure there is a lack of rail cars within this mess, and there is also freight discrimination. But there are other messes as well. The port of Montreal is a mess, but we will clean it up. Our railway access to the port of Vancouver is also a mess, and that will be cleaned up.
Ahead of us in the long and the short term lie exciting challenges. These are challenges which, if properly handled, will ensure that Canada maintains an over-all transportation system which will continue to be unparallelled by the system of any other country in the world. Many forward and positive strides have been made in the past few years. I should like to name a few of them if hon. members will listen. For example, the Ministry of Transport, as it now stands, is structured in such a way that we have better control and integration for planning all modes of transport-central planning for all ports and harbours and a ministry approach which permits decentralization of management but centralization of control.
The positive aspects of a ministry approach are such that all modes are covered, with a central ministry staff that exercises co-ordination over air, marine and all surface modes including urban transit. Integration is essential and that is why the ministry is so structed as to provide integration of all modes. The ministry concept has permitted the creation of the Transport Development Agency, TDA, as a focus for the determination and development of future technological changes in transportation.
Having regard to that aspect, under the old system we had programs which were carried on only by their own momentum. Now we can integrate and direct investments in order to get the best pay-off possible. We can direct money and resources where the need exists. There are no quick and easy solutions. For example, the National Transportation Act needs to be reviewed, and will be reviewed: but the problems are here now and we must face them. We need action here and now, and this is what the minister intends to do.

The role of the ministry is to define national objectives. What are those national objectives? They are a transportation system that is an integral part of regional development-but that is not the only factor. As a resource, like all other resources, a transportation system should be directed in order to achieve social and economic well-being. A transportation system should be reliable and provide reasonably priced transportation services as a fundamental right to all Canadians in all regions of Canada according to their needs. It should guarantee the provision of reliable, low-cost services for the movement of key commodities in the national economy. It should provide a system within which each mode must be allowed to provide those services, and only those, which it does best and in doing so achieve the most efficient utilization of public and private resources.
The transportation system must be responsive to our needs, both in the normal pursuit of our affairs and in times of extraordinary demands. The transportation system must be safe and people must have confidence in that safety. This is also important. It should be a transportation system which will serve Canadians from coast to coast, which will join regions and areas and allow Canadians to become familiar with all sections of Canada and not only some parts. Right now this government is working on all these types of programs and will be presenting legislation in the next few months to take care of the short term. The long-term situation, however, is another matter. But, like all parties, we can see far enough in the future to realize that as much action as is humanly possible must be taken now to minimize the recurrence of these problems in the future. That is what we call the exciting transportation challenge of the months ahead, which includes urban transportation, development of the north, a national port
