Mr. Speaker, it is not unusual for a minister in this government to be highly critical of a former minister in a former government for lack of action and inefficiency as well as failure to meet the problems and so on. I do not suppose that in the parliamentary history of the past 65 years there has been the kind of positive action we have seen in the past couple of weeks. After all, we have had a Liberal government since 1963. We have had a Liberal government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) since 1968. For more than ten years, therefore, the decisions in respect of our transportation policies have been made by Liberal governments on the advice of Liberal ministers of transport.
The present minister has held the position for about a year and a half. Before that we had the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and before that we had the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). Before that we had the man who piloted through the House the present National Transportation Act, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill. If we are in such a hell of a mess, where were these cabinet ministers before? If they were on the job, how could we be in the mess we are in now? We are in a mess because Liberal governments set the kind of policies which we have.
The minister, when he made his great conversion- probably the greatest conversion since Saul was on the way to Damascus-attempted to implicate everybody in the mess. He said all parties were in support of the basic principles of the present transportation act under which we operate our transportation system. Nothing could be further from the truth. This afternoon my leader placed on the record some of the comments made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) back in 1966. I wish to place on the record a few remarks made by the former member for Springfield, the present premier of the province of Manitoba, because he placed his finger on what was wrong with the act. As

recorded at page 11,380 of Hansard December 20, 1966, he said:
They-
The government.
-have put too much faith in competition as an effective means of protecting the public interest.
Then he said:
I think that those regions of this country which produce primary products will be adversely affected by the provisions of this legislation when it becomes law.
We opposed the basic principle of the law then, and still do. Today we brought forth a motion which is being debated at this time which suggests that national transportation should be integrated as a public utility. We heard an attack by the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) which demonstrates clearly the reason the Conservatives very seldom win elections in this country. He demonstrated his ignorance of what goes on in Canada. He talked about public ownership as if it were the most horrible thing in the world, on a day when the Conservative premier of Newfoundland is proposing the nationalization of Brinco. He talks of public ownership as being horrible, at a time when the Conservative government of Alberta is proposing to take a 22 per cent interest in the pipeline in co-operation with the government of Saskatchewan. Since he speaks of public ownership as being something terrible, he should have said this to the present leader of the Conservative Party when he involved this country in a fiasco over heavy water in Cape Breton. It cost the country over $200 million before we produced heavy water.
There is a great deal wrong with the transportation policy of this country. We are not alone in so thinking. I have before me a statement on transportation prepared jointly by the premiers of the four western provinces, including the Hon. Peter Lougheed, Premier of Alberta. Let me read one or two clauses from this statement. Premier Lougheed agrees with the other three premiers in the following:
National policy must recognize that an efficient and adequate transportation system, making the best use of all available modes of transportation, is essential for the economic and social well-being of Canada and its various regions. National transportation policy must recognize that competition at present acts unevenly between the various regions of Canada and between large and small users of transportation services. As a consequence, the development of the western region of Canada is inhibited by the lack of positive policy direction and the discrimination inherent in our present system of freight rates.
That is what the Premier of Alberta had to say. It is almost word for word what our resolution today calls for. That was last July. The premiers asked the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to co-operate with them in reassessing the transportation system and the freight rates system and to make sure that the Canadian Transport Commission and the railways co-operated in this reassessment. They were not being unreasonable. They wanted, on a confidential basis, the actual costs of moving a whole series of important freight items. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport both promised that this information would be made available to the western premiers. Now, seven months later, despite repeated assurances by the Minister of Transport
March 21, 1974

nothing in the way of hard, factual information has been provided to the western premiers.
The Minister of Transport has said publicly that if the railways would not provide this information voluntarily, he would introduce legislation requiring them to do so. No one in this party would object to that kind of legislation. I am sure that the Alberta members of parliament would be the first to urge quick passage of such legislation. If the minister means business, why have we not had that legislation? Mr. Speaker, we have not had it because the minister does not mean business, because he is not really interested in a transportation policy and because he is not really interested in the welfare of the people of the western provinces.
The minister is only interested in picking up an issue which the people of the four western provinces have indicated is important to them and in making speeches which will get support for the Liberal Party in the next election. The minister has had more than enough time to begin to deal with some of the specific cases of discrimination and injustice. He does not need to revamp the whole transportation system, although that is a laudable ambition.
The minister knows the difficulty facing him. He knows how complicated is this country because of its size, geography, sparse population, environmental problems and all the rest. He knows that even if he meant business, he is really talking about something which would take two or three years' work at a minimum. But the people of western Canada are not prepared to wait while the minister makes brilliant speeches and is the subject of laudatory editorials. The people of western Canada, regardless of party, want action and they want it now. The people of western Canada have told the minister, the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission and the Prime Minister the kind of problems with which they must live. They have pointed out that it costs as much to ship steel products from Regina, where a rather substantial steel plant has been built up, to Vancouver as it costs to ship steel from Hamilton to Vancouver. They have pointed out how cheap it is to ship rapeseed from Saskatchewan to Toronto and how expensive it is to ship rapeseed oil, resulting in the processing and associated industries being located in eastern Canada rather than in western Canada where the grain is grown. They have pointed out how much cheaper it is to ship livestock from Calgary to Toronto or Montreal than it is to kill the livestock in the packing plants in Calgary and ship the finished product to Toronto or Montreal. The facts are so clear and abundant that there is no reason for continual delay on the part of the government.
For the minister to speak so glowingly about the need for a new transportation policy is simply to admit the shocking lack of attention and the complete indifference of Liberal governments up until now in dealing with the serious matters that affect western Canadians. The hon. member for Mississauga may think that because these problems are 75 years old they are not important. The fact remains that they have been a cause of dissatisfaction to western Canada from the time the west came into confederation. In fact, they have become more important rather than less important. I have no confidence that the minister
National Transportation Policy and the government will act. They have not acted up until now. They have not dealt with the question of freight rates. They have permitted the railways to destroy the passenger service system: the railways are still continuing that policy.
At present we are involved in the development of a short take-off and landing plant at a cost of $100 million. What will this do? I suppose it will get people from the heart of Ottawa to the heart of Montreal in an hour and a half. But, Mr. Speaker, the railways have been moving people from Ottawa to Montreal in two hours over the last 50 years. Instead of encouraging the railways to upgrade their service and to carry more passengers, the government has permitted them to downgrade passenger service so that people are encouraged to travel from Ottawa to Montreal by any other mode of travel. I use these two locations just as an example. People are encouraged to take a plane, to take a bus; and even with a worldwide shortage of oil, people are encouraged to drive their own cars rather than take a train. We have had another illustration of what the railways and the government think about passenger service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the motion put forward today by the NDP because it gives me a chance to speak once again on what has become my favourite lead-off topic in the House. I do not apologize for my interest in transportation because there is no doubt in my mind that it is the most important single element related to economic policy in Canada. After all, it was the provision of transportation between east and west that brought this country together.
It is shocking that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) should stand in this House and confess that the government has no policy, and that what policy it has, has failed. We have been stumbling along for the past six years without a transportation policy. It is even more shocking to hear his parliamentary secretary somehow blame the opposition for this lack of transportation policy. He seems to forget that his party has been in power for ten years. His party passed the National Transportation Act. His party has been responsible for administering that act. Surely he is reaching for extremes, reaching for the clouds when he tries to place the blame on the opposition.
After that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) got up and stated categorically that he has no faith in the present minstry, that he does not believe they are capable of enacting proper legislation and that even if they had the legislation, he doubted they would enforce it. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I simply ask him: Why do you keep this crowd in power? You have had your chance, and you are doing nothing.
If there was any question of the urgency of this problem, the fact that we ran into a simulated oil energy crisis is an example. It turned out not to be a crisis of supply but a crisis of transportation. In its shortsightedness, this government had not provided facilities to move the oil

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
from the west to the east. There is also the fact that we ran into a wheat transportation crisis because, again, in its lack of wisdom and failure to formulate a proper policy this government has not provided the facilities to move the grain to the ports so that it can be shipped to the export markets which we have developed.
The crisis is here, the problem is here, and this motion is very appropriate at this time. I agree with the premise of the motion, that we need some sort of policy to end indiscriminate rail line abandonment, to do something about supplying new, modern equipment to move goods and get passenger service back where it should be. I agree with all those things, and action should be taken to get us out of this mess.
Having said that I agree with the objective of the motion, my agreement with the party that proposed it ends. I certainly do not agree with the approach my socialist friends would take. It is too easy. They always say that if something is not working, it should be nationalized. But surely we have had a great deal of experience in this country and know what happens when something is turned over to a Crown corporation. We have seen the horrible mess in the Post Office. Surely any business operated as that one is would not long survive. We saw what happened with the waste and duplication in Manpower offices. Also, there is the horrible example of the CBC. But the thing that disturbs me most, Mr. Speaker, was referred to briefly by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) earlier today: it is all right to talk about public ownership, but judging from what I have seen during my time in this parliament, once something is turned over to public ownership the public loses all control of it.
We have had examples of this in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications when officials of the CNR and Air Canada have appeared. We have watched them deliberately dodge questions when they did not want to give information on the operation of those companies. Surely this information should be public knowledge and at least available to the representatives of the people. We have seen what happens when Crown corporations are set up: parliamentary control is lost. This does not make me very receptive to any suggestion of further nationalization of our transportation system.
In his speech on March 7, when he first admitted that things were in such a mess, the minister told us what we in the opposition have been telling the government for six years; things, incidentally, that everybody knew. I do not know why it took the minister so long to become aware that the transportation policy had broken down, but at least we can give him full marks for admitting it in public in the House. I cannot agree with all that the minister says because I do not think he can lay all the blame for this breakdown on the legislation. I feel that there is statutory authority both in the Railway Act and in the National Transportation Act which gives the minister the power to force the railways to move grain when necessary. There is power in the National Transportation Act under Section 3(2) and section 26 for the CTC to act if it is felt that the carriers are discriminating against any particular region. These are powers that the minister has not used, Mr. 
Speaker, and this is my chief criticism of the minister and the government.
In committee we have heard from the CNR and Air Canada. They complain and criticize and say, "If only someone in the government would define and delineate our responsibilities . . . " The minister's appointee, Mr. Pratt, made this statement two or three years ago. He said that Air Canada was prepared to carry out its responsibilities if only the minister or someone in government would define which routes would be operated on a public service basis and which on a profit basis. The president of Canadian National Railways has said the same thing. It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that while the existing legislation is not perfect, there are powers that can be used; therefore, this minister and this government are derelict in their duty because they have not used those powers. They have not said to the carriers, "This is your responsibility. This you must do."
I should like now to refer briefly to another matter of policy which has disturbed me greatly. This is another example of the government's failure to give direction. I was very pleased when the hon. member for Verdum (Mr. Mackasey) referred to CNR pensions today. I know that, with his vast experience in labour relations, he is a man who is entirely sympathetic to the underdog and he has always tried to give help where necessary. The hon. member referred to the sad situation existing in the original pension plan, the provident fund or, as we in the maritimes know it, the ICR pension plan. It is unbelievable that former employees of Crown corporations or quasi-Crown corporations should be expected to live under the conditions that these pensioners have been enduring for the past ten or fifteen years since they retired. It is unbelievable in this day and age that many of these people retire on a pension as low as $25, and when they die their widows are cut right off, or maybe left with $5 and-as the hon. member for Verdun mentioned-they take 10 per cent off that.
The sad thing is that there are so few of these people that it would not cost very much to give them something extra to bring them in line with present-day costs. I have not estimated the amount, but in the over-all budget of this government it would be infinitesimal. I have heard it said that there might only be about 2,000 of them altogether, and maybe 40 or 50 still working for the railway. There may be 40 or 50 widows, but those widows have no pension at all. I know the minister has compassion for people, and I know the parliamentary secretary is interested in this problem because I have talked to him about it. Here is an area where the government can give direction to the CNR and other Crown corporations. Surely there must be a way to bring some measure of justice to these people who have been deserted by the unions and the company. I call upon the minister and his parliamentary secretary to look into this problem.
We hear the argument that the National Transportation Act has broken down because it is based solely on the profit motive. I do not agree with that entirely, but we cannot disregard that motive. There is no reason why a company, whether a Crown corporation or a private corporation, should not be operated efficiently and pay its way. But in a country such as ours, with regions where a
March 21, 1974

rail line or airline cannot make a profit, such areas should be delineated as public service runs and supported from the general treasury.
This idea of phasing out the profit motive and running everything as a Crown corporation is hogwash; you have to operate a business and make a profit where it can be made. This was brought home to me a few weeks ago when the CTC held hearings on the efficiency of air services. In brief after brief the complaint was made that service in the area was not adequate because the main carrier, Air Canada, had no competition and as a result service had run down to the point where actually there was no service; In other words, if there is to be service there must be competition.
May I refer briefly to something the minister mentioned this afternoon. The great weakness of the National Transportation Act is that it makes no provision for regulatory authorities to supervise carriers in order to make sure they give efficient service. The minister referred to the subsidies the railways receive. Yet there is nothing to force them to upgrade service or to buy new equipment. This matter should be looked into. A regulatory body ought to be set up which on a day to day basis will make sure that efficient service is provided.
I could say much more on this topic, Mr. Speaker, but in my limited time I wish to say that I feel the Minister of Transport is sincere in wanting to clean up this mess. I know he is disturbed because the government has let transportation policy deteriorate to this point. Yet I remind the parliamentary secretary that we on this side are somewhat skeptical when we hear promises, promises but see no action. Only two years ago the previous minister of transport said in the House that he would immediately bring in an entirely new transportation policy. We have not yet seen it. Is it any wonder that we grow skeptical when the minister says he will bring in a new policy?
I feel that the legislation the previous minister had in mind was blocked either by the cabinet or by officials in the department. If these officials still have their jobs, they will continue blocking action which the present minister might take. As he does not have sufficient power to correct the ills of the transportation system, I feel that new legislation should be passed to give him that power. If he is honestly and sincerely trying to clean up this horrible mess, he can count on my full and complete co-operation in rushing the legislation through.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying how pleased I am to have heard what the minister announced today and during the previous few days. He admits that there is something seriously wrong with our transport system. That is the only way you can straighten out a difficulty: first you must admit there is something wrong, and then you work toward realigning transportation policy by bringing in a new set of policies which will be relevant for Canadians. I shall examine some of the problems inherent in our transport system and I shall confine my thoughts first to railroads and then deal with intermodal possibilities. The root of the problem is
National Transportation Policy the National Transportation Act of 1967, as the minister admitted. There is general agreement about this.
We must face the difficulty that parliament lacks control over our transportation system. Neither the minister nor parliament can exercise direct control over the CTC.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
We have already dealt with that. As I said, the CTC tends to behave like other regulatory bodies in that it has become sympathetic to the views of those it is regulating. That seems to be the basic difficulty. Not long after you appoint new people to the CTC, they begin to speak and think as if they are operating a railroad. You can make similar observations about other regulatory bodies. There is a great body of literature about regulators.
I think the minister, the government and parliament must assume more power in order to control transportation, particularly in view of our difficulties in moving grain and lumber this year. At Thunder Bay, there are many problems connected with grain movement, with elevators being only half full when at this time of year they should be pretty well topped up.
Our second problem which concerns the act itself is the whole notion that transportation must pay, must be competitive and must be based on competition. I do not think that is a reliable policy in a country as broad as Canada, as thinly populated as Canada. It just does not work. Although competition may work in some areas, I am not sure that we really understand the effects of competition on the railroads.
As I said, I shall also be talking about intermodal systems. It seems to me that the underlying feature of the act should be in the preamble, which should say that the act shall be designed to redistribute growth throughout the country and bring equality to the regions of the country suffering from disparity. That ought to be the aim of our transportation system. A competitive system may work if it serves Toronto, Montreal and the golden horseshoe, but it does not work in the maritimes or the outer areas of this country. With these thoughts in mind, the act ought to be changed. It should take cognizance of the notion that transportation systems should be designed to bring equality to all parts of this country. That notion is missing from the act and from the regulations governing the CTC. As a result we see massive problems in the field of freight rates. It is much cheaper, for instance, to move cargoes west than to move them east. It is cheaper to move cattle on the hoof east than to move the finished product east. Anomalies like that must be removed. I know it will not be simple to sort out freight rates, but these anomalies stem from the present act.
Something else which disturbs me is how the railroads get subsidies. How do they get them? They apply for discontinuance and then downgrade the passenger service.

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
It is anathema to me that a railroad should get a subsidy after it has downgraded the service. To prevent its discontinuance after the service has been downgraded, the subsidy is granted. As the previous speaker mentioned, such a system encourages the downgrading of service. In other words, the subsidy is provided for not giving service. This must be changed.
During the recess I had the pleasure of taking my family by rail to the west coast. We went out by Canadian National and came back by Canadian Pacific. The trip was interesting. I went to find out what was happening and to talk to as many railroaders as possible at various points. I had great difficulty in getting a bedroom on the Super Continental. When we got on the train there were already 15 cars well filled. The bedroom rate was $126 and the fare was $67, so that the one-way trip cost us $193. As I say, the train was full; it was hard to get reservations. They had to put on an extra car at Winnipeg. This was even though we travelled in mid-February. I must say this: the food was good, the service was good and a definite attempt was made to accommodate people who could not afford sleeping car accommodation. They had what is known as a day and night car on the train for which the price was reasonable, about $8.
The story of the CP train was entirely different. The fare cost us $232, for example, almost $40 more than the CN fare. There were seven cars on the CP train, with four or five people in each car. The company was not being at all competitive. I heard Conservatives talking about competition and about how wonderful CP is and how bad the CN is. Let me tell them there was no comparison between the services. As far as I am concerned, if there is a way to do this I will move that the subsidy for The Canadian of the CPR be reduced to $1 because they really are not doing their job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
I just do not grab this thing. Because it is private enterprise, it is bound to be good. Because it is public, it is bound to be bad. Although there are inefficiencies and problems with CNR, they are trying. But the CPR does not give a damn. As far as I am concerned, there should be no subsidy for CPR.
I wish to deal with some other problems. They do not deal specifically with the act but they are basic problems in the transportation system. Neither railroad is aggressive. This is one of the problems. They are not aggressive in comparison with other segments of our industry. Where were the railroads when we were talking about the Pickering airport scheme? Where were the railroads when a ground transportation scheme was an alternative? Where were they when STOL was being considered? They were not there. Where was the privately-owned CPR? The railroads have not been aggressive in the same way as other industries.
International Nickel in my area has a mine in Shebando-wan, a mile or two from the CN siding. The ore is being trucked to a CP siding 50 miles away. The province of Ontario had to spend a great deal of money to reinforce the highway. There had been a series of accidents. This
[Mr. McRae.l
could have been taken to a CN siding for a small amount of money. Where are the aggressive railroads we should have in this country? This is a very serious problem.
I do not, however, blame the railroads entirely for all the problems that occurred this winter. One interesting feature of our trip is that we arrived in Kamloops six hours late. That was because on almost every siding on the north line CN had a freight train or we were sitting waiting for a freight train. I was told by employees that with one or two more trains the system would break down. CN is carrying a tremendous load. This heavy demand was creating some of the problems we were running into last winter.
I wish to talk about another problem. This has not been looked at as carefully as it might have been. I refer to the whole notion of intermodal aspects of transportation. It is the user who pays, or is it the state? When we talk about competition between truckers and railroads, are we really using similar cost figures? I cannot find decent cost figures. I can find figures based on the cost per ton-mile but I cannot find cost figures that say: In order to put a 50 ton truck on the road, it will cost so much more to build a suitable highway and maintain it. This kind of figure does not exist. I do not think we have done a decent job of understanding relating figures. Certainly of late there has been a move away from trucking and toward rail, particularly the notion of piggyback.
The other aspect of the intermodal situation we have not looked at is energy consumption. Up until now we have only talked about cost. We now have to consider the cost of energy and energy consumption. In this regard rail is certainly a far more efficient system. In terms of gross tonnage, for rail it is about 550 ton-miles per gallon. The highway user gets about 38 ton-miles per gallon, and the air user about 30 ton-miles per gallon. In terms of net tonnage the ratio is about four to one; 210 ton-miles for a railroad and about 50 ton-miles per gallon for a truck. This is another factor that has to be looked at very seriously. In terms of energy, the railways are far more efficient.
The intermodal form of transportation, the pipeline, has not been discussed in this debate. I give notice here and now that I am not at all happy about the building of the Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline. There are all kinds of problems with that, but that is another story for a future debate. In conclusion, I wish to go over what I think, needs to be done. First, control of our transportation system, particularly our railways, must be put back in the hands of parliament. Second, there must be a preamble to the act which states that one of the major functions of railroads in this country is to redistribute growth and move goods back and forth with some equality so that all areas of Canada have equal economic opportunities. Third, the subsidy for passenger service should be a subsidy for service, not taking away service. It should not be based on a system of asking to remove a service. Fourth, management must be made aggressive.
The federal government will have to assert a great deal more control and perhaps take over ownership also. In some way the railways must become more aggressive. Fifth, a much more careful study must be made of the rationalization of costs and energy use in terms of the intermodal use of our transportation system.
March 21, 1974

This country is very fragile. It is far too difficult a country to put together when railroads and our transportation system in general is not working. We cannot afford the luxury of railroads that do not care. Our railroads must be aggressive. They must work for Canadians. The control should be put back in the hands of parliament where it belongs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years I have listened to various parties discuss the problem raised today by the New Democratic Party, namely, the development of a transportation policy. I think it would be possible to take a motion that was moved ten years ago and put it today; I am sure there would be great similarity between it and the motion we are presently debating.
Governments do not have too great an opportunity to make a mark and ministers usually do not have a very great opportunity to make a mark in history. However, if the minister really understands what he said in the past few days, namely, that we have no national transportation policy and he is fed up with the fact he cannot provide boxcars to move national produce across our nation, he will do something. If he has been watching Pierre Berton reliving, or rewriting history, and if he wants to join Pierre Berton in the second episode of the National Dream, he will try to do something about what we have suggested.
If we are going to do anything about transportation in this nation, we will have to unite all rail transportation into one unit and make it a viable force. We will have to put great effort into making the railways our national transportation system for now and for many years to come.
I note that the National Energy Board has been presented with the first batch of 200 pounds of documents concerning transportation facilities. They do not count them any more by the number of pages; they weigh them. This concerns the Mackenzie Valley pipeline proposal. If the dream of the government at the time of confederation had any merit, Canadians would be well advised to take a close look at this proposition and determine whether or not a railway would be the answer to bringing our resources out of the far north.
A few years ago the Russians came to this country and were impressed by our transportation system. They were developing an industrial complex in their northern region and they felt Canadians had great expertise in the transportation field. If they were to return today, 15 years later, they would find we have gone backward instead of forward. Some of our troubles are caused by the fact that transportation system is so complex. We are experimenting with small STOL aircraft. There could not be a poorer designation for an Otter aircraft than to call it a STOL aircraft. The Otter is the old Norseman, but with two engines instead of one. It is an aircraft built primarily for bush operations. Yet we propose to use it to move passengers between Ottawa and Montreal, 18 at a time, and consider this to be a step forward. It is not a step forward, it is a step backward. We are moving a bush pilot operation into the cities now, plying between cities instead of between remote rural points. A great deal of money has
National Transportation Policy been spent on this project. Rockcliffe airport has been revitalized, as has the Expo airstrip in Montreal. The point is, we have dissipated our abilities in the transportation field.
If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) wants to do anything at all, I suggest he concentrate on the railroads. I think it is possible that if he were to ask the Canadian Pacific Railway to give him the railway, lock, stock and barrel, it would probably do so because those people are not interested in the railroad business. I am sure they do not have the capital invested in it nor, any more, the experts who can run it. They are interested in diversification, in industries and operations which produce far more money for them than the railroad has ever produced. The only advantage they get out of the railway is the product of the millions of dollars the Canadian people gave them, money they have used, not to maintain the railroad but to reinvest in other directions, making a pot of money in the process.
The railway operation is the poor cousin, and we are continually asked to subsidize it. The railway service should be nationalized. I believe we ought to nationalize not only the Canadian Pacific but the Canadian National as well. The president of the CNR has appeared before the railway committee on a number of occasions. He could not even tell us what the directors were supposed to be doing. One of them is responsible for the communications tower in Toronto-the needle. How will that project help operate a railroad? We must divest the railroads of the other operations in which they are engaged. I think this involves the trucking operation too, though this is open for debate; it might be that there is advantage in running a trucking operation together with the railroad.
I spoke to a senior official of the Ontario Northland railroad some time after the bad accident which took place on Highway 401 in which a number of people were killed following a collision between a truck from my area, a bus and 13 or 14 other vehicles. He told me that the Northland railway could put on trains, particularly at weekends, which could move trucks and trailers of the kind involved in the accident directly into Toronto by rail, taking this traffic off the highway and making a profit both for the truckers and for the railroad.
There is much that could be done along these lines, but if the minister intends to do anything to improve the system he should devote his attention only to the railroads. I believe we can upgrade our railroads. We could investigate new types of rolling stock, though here again there may be setbacks. I am sure we are the laughing stock of the world, having spent millions of dollars on the rapid transit system between Montreal and Toronto only to find we have not been able to match the Silver Bullet which operated some 30 years ago between Buffalo and Detroit and which could even take on water while travelling at 60 miles an hour. We have not been able to match this, and why? The CN is really more interested in its investment portfolio than it is in running a railroad.
Last year I opposed Air Canada buying into the air charter business through Wardair. I would have been happy if the intention was to buy Wardair and operate it as an airline, because I think Air Canada should be flying airplanes. But the idea was to establish an investment

March 21, 1974
National Transportation Policy
portfolio. The idea, now, is to buy into Comstock. I remember Comstock as the organization which changed electric motors over from 25 cycles to 60 cycles right across Ontario. I am sure they have a lot of expertise in the aircraft industry. But Air Canada proposes to buy into it. Is this because it plans to fly De Havilland aircraft, or Otters? I doubt it. They are going to buy into it because it is an investment, and I am utterly opposed to the corporation getting into this field. If Air Canada wants to fly airplanes and be a national airline, let it stick to being a national airline, without letting third-rate carriers get into the feeder line business.
The same is true of the railways. If we were so stupid as to allow the Canadian Wheat Board to put up $400 million to buy 20,000 hopper cars-

speechtext: Four thousand.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
My hon. friend says 4,000. They already have
4.000.	They have 4,000 now and the order is in for another
2.000.	Over the next five years they want 20,000, at a cost of $400 million. My colleague does not know, but he did not attend many of the meetings where the Wheat Board made this request. In fact, they requested 20,000 cars, and the potash industry received $39 million from the government to buy hopper cars.
The premiers of the western provinces ask the federal government to upgrade roadbeds because they are unable to bear the loads of today. I suggest we will be establishing a third new railway system, one that has no engines. I imagine someone will come along shortly and say, "Let us give the Wheat Board some engines and some employees". Then the potash industry will ask for some engines. So we will be providing the rolling stock and the roadbed, and the railroads are going to haul our cars because they do not have their own. In Regina they were burning cars, but agreed to allow the federal government to select some of them and fix them up. Canadian National offered to pay 50 per cent of the cost, but Canadian Pacific said the government would have to pay 100 per cent of the cost and pay for the scrap as well. If the minister is going to do anything at all for Pierre Berton, and if there is going to be a sequel to the great national dream, then something must be done about the great national tragedy of today where there are not enough cars to haul the freight of the nation.
There is no question that passenger service on the railways today is a disgrace. Anyone who has recently travelled on a train will have discovered they were travelling on the same cars that were used during the war. There have been no new passenger cars put on our railways for years and years. It costs as much for a sleeper on the CNR today as it does to stay at the Royal York Hotel.
In closing, if the minister wants to make a name for himself, he will get the support of the Canadian people and other members of this House if he will concentrate on making the railway system of Canada a viable unit, making this unit, as Mussolini did, run on time and provide service to the Canadian people, something the railways are not doing at the present time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this opposition day on the motion proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) on behalf of his party. One of the main things I have become more aware of over the years is transportation, and the CPR has been foremost in this respect. I am reminded of the story that I once heard and believed to be true, that when the hon. member for York South was appearing before the board that was selecting Rhodes scholars, one of the board members, who was president of the CPR at the time, asked him what he would do with the CPR if he had the chance. The hon. member replied, "I would nationalize it". Now, some 30 years later, he is still taking up the same cause.
My involvement with the CPR started very early in my life. The hon. member for York South talked today about the land that the CPR was given by the Canadian people. I happen to have been born and raised on one of these sections of land and I was there for about 21 years. I ran a farm and in the last few years before I joined the air force we had, in my opinion, a fair deal from the CPR, especially during the thirties when it was very hard even to make any kind of payment. I should like to remind hon. members what land costs today in the province of British Columbia since the NDP government has taken over. I am sure the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) knows full well of what I am saying.
There are certainly many problems in our transportation system. It seems to me that to say they can all be solved by nationalization is a gross oversimplification. The problems are very real and must be faced with determination. I can tell the House from experiences I have had with the CPR on many occasions that I have found them superior to the CNR. During some 13 trips that I made in wartime over the Rocky Mountain passes from the prairies to Vancouver, I always found the CPR superior in every way to the CNR. During the change from reefer cars to mechanical cars, the CPR at least constructed new cars and made them large enough to conform to Canadian and United States regulations, whereas the CNR did a great deal of converting of cars. Thus the load limits of their cars are too small. Both of these railway companies, however, have let Canada down. The CNR, in my opinion, is certainly no example, and if nationalization is the answer, then they should be.
I get many complaints from my constituents regarding the mail service that is run by the Post Office, a government department. The Post Office had a program of assured mail. The program was supposed to assure prompt delivery, yet letters took anywhere from a week to ten days to come to my home town from Vancouver, 300 miles away. This shows lack of leadership. If we are to have nationalization and government-owned companies, they should be setting the example.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has finally recognized that truth of what I said in the transport committee on November 20 last year when the president of the CNR was a witness. As reported at page 20:92 of the committee proceedings, I said:
I know that there are two railways. The CPR is almost as bad. I would certainly be recommending that the CNR people go on the block and sell to a private enterprise, but here we have a private enterprise that cannot do very much better.
March 21, 1974

It has come to the point, to my way of thinking, that the railways are really telling the government. The government is not telling the railways. Probably the person in the government that I should be talking to is the Minister of Transport, because I think it is high time this government sould be doing something about telling the railways and making sure that they have the rolling stock and have the cars.
In the fruit and lumber industry there is a crucial < shortage of cars in British Columbia to haul the products. The railways are recommending that the companies buy or lease cars themselves. It almost appears as if the shortage is deliberate so they can force or bully these companies into buying cars, thus freeing them from any responsibility to do so. This is a responsibility that I believe must rest with the railways. Once they have bought cars, I would not trust the railways even to return the cars to their original destination. The next step would be for the railways to say, "Now you have bought the cars, you may as well buy engines too". This is not what I would call showing responsibility. Certainly the government should see to it that the railways carry out their responsibilities. The railways should be told they will not receive any subsidy unless they listen to what the government says. Instead, the government allows the railway companies to operate on tax dollars in spite of the fact that one of them is already government-owned. Perhaps it should hold back these grants in the hope that this might make more responsive the attitude of the railways to government demands.
I am very pleased to see that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) is here this evening and I hope he will listen to my remarks. We had a problem in my constituency as a result of which we were sending products to the United States and shipping them on U.S. railways to eastern Canada because we could not get rail cars from a Canadian carrier. Suddenly there was an order issued that Customs officers should not go down to seal these cars. I think the excuse given was that it was too costly, even though the U.S. carrier was prepared to pay the cost of the trip of the Customs officers in order that the cars could go through the United States. This was being done on a short line of the Burlington Northern Railway which was running into Canada. A bridge had been washed out on the rail line and they were loading cars for us and shipping out of a small point just below the border. I suspect it was this action by the railway that caused the government to take certain action.
Let me read from a letter I received from the Minister of National Revenue as follows:
Originally we were advised by the Canadian railroad that they could supply the required rolling stock.
I do not know which railroad he meant by that. He went on to say:
Subsequently it was ascertained that there was, in fact, a scarcity of reefer cars in British Columbia and the railroad could only look after their regular customers.
There certainly was a shortage of reefer cars in Canada, but as far as we were concerned we had always been a regular customer. The minister continued:
-it would seem prudent for B.C. Tree Fruits Limited to get in touch with Canadian carriers to discuss their requirements for rolling stock
National Transportation Policy
so that they will be considered as "regular customers" and the problem can be eliminated.
It is very evident that Canadian railways still cannot supply sufficient rolling stock and that is the reason there is a shortage about which the grain people are complaining. It is for that reason the lumber people, the fruit people and almost anyone you might consider is complaining about rail service in Canada. Our grain shippers are surely regular customers of the railways. Perhaps they should be told to get in touch with these companies in respect of their requirements, in order that they can be considered as regular customers. The minister should and must know that these people are all regular customers. There is a problem but it will never be solved by that kind of action or that kind of statement.
If we are to solve these problems, the government must become more responsive to our needs and take stronger action. If that were the case, I suggest we would not be told that nationalization is the cure-all for everything. We must put the onus on these carriers, and we must take a hard line with them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY, NATIONALIZATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AND APPOINTMENT OF CONTROLLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the debate on the CNR bill in 1968 I suggested that the trouble with the CNR was that there were too many chiefs and not enough Indians. Tonight I suggest that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) should fire the chiefs and let the Indians take over. I am sure that then the railways would be operated at 100 per cent efficiency, because the workers are transportation men, they know the transportation business and they could rectify the problems we are now facing. They could provide the services and the CNR would make a lot more money. These men have spent their lives in the railway business, whereas the officials have not.
During the past winter a man told me that there were no cars and no locomotives available because they were being held away from home at terminals for up to 24 hours. What a way to run a railroad! Certainly the CPR makes money because it takes only the cream and leaves the milk for the public system. There was no money in passenger business, and the CPR gave the public system what was left after it had done with it.
Canada is a large country and the CNR has to take the good with the bad and provide service to areas which the CPR will not handle. Between Windsor and the United States border the Canadian Pacific Railway makes plenty of money on their short and long haul freight runs, as nearly all the traffic is long-haul and the CNR has to look after the short as well as the long haul runs between Sarnia and Portland, Maine.
If a person buys stock in a company, he has the right to attend the annual meetings and question the president and officials about the operations of that company. However, thousands of railway employees pay into pension plans but are not supplied with any information about the type of investments made. The employees could not care less where the money is invested, but surely they should receive an annual statement showing a list of those investments and the interest made. All the employees are asking for is open books and proof that the CNR and CPR pension funds are not generating a 2 per cent pension per year of

March 21, 1974
Adjournment Debate
service. We should give the employees of the CN and CP and other railways the facts and let them decide what they want done with their pension funds. Surely these employees have a right to know where their money is being invested and at what rate.
Canada does not have a deep-sea merchant marine. The government is, however, taking the first step toward strengthening and enlarging our small fleet by closing the coastal trade to all but Canadian vessels. Legislation will soon be introduced to make this effective. Nevertheless, this legislation will take into consideration the fact that parts of Canada, especially the eastern provinces, are dependent upon water-borne transportation and the viability of their enterprises may depend on the lowest possible rates by water.
A second step to enlarge our fleet may occur in Arctic regions, where Canadian resources should be exploited by Canadian technology, giving rise to Canadian enterprise and employing Canadian labour. None of the major shipping countries of the world has vessels that can operate safely in the Canadian Arctic except for a few months a year. The ministry is currently devising ways and means of encouraging Canadian enterprise to take up the challenge of operating Canadian flag vessels in our Arctic on an extended season basis.
In the past, Canada has bought its deep-sea transportation at economical rates from the lowest bidders, whether they be Liberian vessels, British Commonwealth vessels or Russian vessels. This has been favourable costwise and ships have always been available. The changing pattern of world shipping must now be studied to determine whether Canada will be able effectively to continue marketing its products worldwide and at a reasonable cost without any ships of its own.

subtopic: HEALTH-PRESENCE OF DES IN UNITED STATES CATTLE IMPORTED INTO CANADA
HEALTH-PRESENCE OF DES IN UNITED STATES CATTLE IMPORTED INTO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks tonight are addressed to both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). On two separate occasions, on February 28 and March 6, I tried to get an answer from these ministers on a question of vital concern to all Canadian consumers. I asked what the government was doing to ensure that no beef would be imported from the

United States which came from cattle fattened with the chemical agent DES.
Reliable evidence has been available for some months that the chemical DES causes cancer in both humans and animals, and on the basis of that information the present government banned the use of DES in this country. In the meantime, the United States supreme court handed down a decision overthrowing the ban on its use in that country and this has raised a very serious question. It means that there is a danger that DES-treated beef can be imported into Canada and pose a threat to the health of Canadian citizens. That is my concern in this matter.
I thought that, between the two ministers, I would have received some assurance that the government had worked out this problem at about the same time the ban on the use of DES in Canada was imposed. However, Mr. Speaker, it now appears that nothing was done. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said on March 6 that necessary steps would be taken to ensure that DES-treated beef would not enter Canada. That was not good enough. He should have said that necessary steps had been taken months ago. It would appear that the health of our citizens is less important to the minister than football franchises.
When the use of DES was banned in the United States there was no guarantee that all beef producers in that country stopped using it as a feed additive. There is no way in which we can know whether or not we have been importing DES-treated beef during the period of the ban, because we have not required exporters in the United States to certify that every beef carcass had been inspected and found to be free of DES. Traces of the chemical can only be detected in the livers of slaughtered cattle, and even then slight traces of DES can go undetected unless very careful tests are made.
I heard recently that the government will undertake spot checks of beef being imported from the United States to ensure that none of it contains DES. This falls far short of what is needed. We cannot do less than demand that every carcass intended for export to Canada is checked and certified. We must insist that the liver test be made on all beef intended for export to this country, and that could not be made at border points. Last year, for instance, we imported 160 million pounds of retail cuts of beef from the United States, and it is obvious that the tests must have been made at the slaughterhouses under United States government supervision.
We cannot do less than demand that guarantee, Mr. Speaker. I think it was in 1952 that we had a serious outbreak of hoof and mouth disease in the western provinces, and the U.S. imposed a total ban on beef imports from Canada until they got assurances that Canada was free of the disease. When a health hazard is known or even suspected in imported foods, the United States government does not hesitate to erect the necessary safeguards for their citizens. Why should we be prepared to do less for our citizens?
Mr. Speaker, we are told that there are two ways that DES can be used to fatten cattle. The first is the way I have already mentioned, and that is by adding DES to the feed. The other way is what is called an ear implant: the chemical is implanted in the ear of the cattle. This can be done many times during the period the animal is being
March 21, 1974

fattened. It is widely believed that the marks of DES implants can be detected on the ear of a slaughtered animal, but while it might be possible in some cases it is not a sure test. And even if we could assume that it would be a valid test, there would still be animals that were given DES in their feed. In those cases we should have assurances that tests had been made on the livers of the slaughtered animals.
We should not lose any more time in setting up some kind of arrangement whereby the United States government would certify that all beef exported to Canada had been tested at the slaughter-house and found to be free of any trace of DES. We cannot, and must not settle for less than that, Mr. Speaker.
It is significant to note that the U.S. court did not overthrow the ban on the use of DES because the hazard to human health had not been proven. It was overthrown on a purely legal point in that the U.S. food and drug administration had not held public hearings on the issue before the ban was imposed. The ban was imposed on the basis that DES presented a hazard to human health, and there is good reason to suppose that a ban will be imposed again in that country as soon as the legal niceties have been ironed out.
In the meantime, no one in Canada can be sure that DES-treated beef will not show up on food counters. In fact, we cannot even be sure that we have not been eating DES-treated beef during the entire period of the ban in our country, which dates from January, 1973. This is an appalling situation and one that cannot be passed over with the answer that some day, someone in the government is going to do something about it.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have been irresponsible in the handling of this matter. They made the assumption that all U.S. beef producers would discontinue the use of DES during the period of the ban, and therefore all beef that we have imported from the U.S. has been free of the chemical. That was a dangerous assumption.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-PRESENCE OF DES IN UNITED STATES CATTLE IMPORTED INTO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott) and would like to point out that on March 6, 1974, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) responded to the hon. member's question, he indicated that there would be no importation of DES-implanted beef into Canada. That decision still stands.
I do not think it is really fair or responsible to become so alarmist as to indicate that people have been eating DES-treated beef when there is just no evidence to show that that has been so. The Department of National Health and Welfare is very deeply concerned with the health of Canadians, and it has been concerned with this question for a considerable length of time.
As the hon. member pointed out, up until the decision was made by the supreme court in the United States on January 26 to throw out the embargo on the use of DES in that country, it would have been unreasonable to think that some farmer, either an American or a farmer in any
Adjournment Debate
other part of the world, would have been so silly as to run the risk of destroying all his herd by implanting DES when such beef was not allowed to be sold in the U.S. or in Canada. I have a considerable number of rural people in my riding, just as the hon. member has in his, and they are certainly not dumb enough to do anything like that; and I do not think American farmers are that dumb, either.
In any event, we in the Department of National Health and Welfare have an inspection branch which is responsible for this kind of health question. It is not under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture at all. The Minister of Agriculture is concerned with the protection of farmers and with the quality of beef that is imported, but is certainly not directly involved in how it might affect the health of Canadians. That is our responsibility. We are discharging that responsibility. We have said that no beef implanted with DES will be allowed into this country. We are making representations this week to the Americans, through the Department of Agriculture, informing them that we want primary certification in respect of any beef that will be brought into Canada from the U.S. or else we will have to close down the border to imports of beef. I think that is a pretty strong and determined stand that we have taken.
We are concerned about the problem. We are certain DES-implanted beef has not arrived in this country to date, and there is no way it will be available to come in until May 24, 120 days after the ban in the U.S. was lifted. We assure Canadians, including all members of this House, that DES-implanted beef will not be allowed into this country under any circumstances.

subtopic: ENERGY-REASON IMPERIAL OIL ALLOWED TO DRILL FOR OIL AND GAS IN BEAUFORT SEA BEFORE COMPLETION OF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
ENERGY-REASON IMPERIAL OIL ALLOWED TO DRILL FOR OIL AND GAS IN BEAUFORT SEA BEFORE COMPLETION OF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight on the subject of gas drilling in the Beaufort Sea, a matter which seemed to upset the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) when I brought it up last week. It was just last week that the minister claimed that a heap of silt dredged from the floor of Shallow Bay is an island. In a moment or two I will be returning to the subject of this so-called island.
Today, tears of joy must have come to the eyes of various ministers as a long awaited dream came true and an application was presented to the National Energy Board to export natural gas from the Mackenzie Delta. This project evidently has the support of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself. Last December, dreaming of all the precious gas reserves that might one day be sent south of the border via a Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline, the Prime Minister declared to the House:
The government believes that it would be in the public interest to facilitate early construction by any means which do not require the lowering of environmental standards or the neglect of Indian rights and interests.
One would hope that environmental standards and native rights would be of some importance in the drilling for this gas which the government seems to eager to export, but there is some question as to whether this is the case in the drillings now going on in the Beaufort Sea.

Two weeks ago we were told that the government would allow no offshore drilling until environmental studies are completed, two years from now. At about the same time we learned that Imperial Oil had made a substantial find after drilling from a man-made offshore sand bar in the Beaufort Sea. But this was not offshore, insisted the minister; this was an island. Imperial Oil named it Adgo, or something like that. I suggest that after the spring breakup the island will no longer be there, so I call it a sand bar.
Oilweek, the government's favourite ecology magazine, stated on page 17 of its March 4 issue that Adgo is, and I quote:
-made of dredged silt, now frozen. It will "self-destruct" during spring break-up.
Mr. Speaker, it will disappear like the sand bars in the Mackenzie River which I have seen disappear after a flood and perhaps reappear further downstream.
It would appear that the only purpose of building the island at all was to snow the minister and his people who advised the Tuktoyaktuk council to grant a land use permit. A land use permit to drill for gas in the Beaufort Sea! The minister knows, or ought to know, that if a blow-out occurs it will take between four and eight months to drill a relief well. That can mean a lot of gas, and maybe oil too, in the Beaufort Sea. And is this such a far-fetched possibility? Imperial's first island well, Immerk, had to be capped after drilling to a depth of 7,000 feet because of the intense pressures encountered, well above the level at which they said this could happen. As Oilweek put it:
Geopressures will continue to cause moments of excitement as drillers attempt to harness high pressure zones.
Mr. Speaker, I hate the thought that at every "moment of excitement" serious damage may be threatened to the environment and to the native peoples of whose heritage it forms such an important part. I should like the minister to produce the environmental studies on the basis of which the government allowed the Beaufort Sea drilling to go ahead. I believe this would be a minimal indication of the government's sincerity in protecting environmental standards and native rights. If not, it will become very plain that the government speaks with a forked tongue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ENERGY-REASON IMPERIAL OIL ALLOWED TO DRILL FOR OIL AND GAS IN BEAUFORT SEA BEFORE COMPLETION OF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member rose tonight, but I am a bit surprised by the tone of his remarks because he is the member for the Northwest Territories and should be happy that we were
right when we gave the permit to drill from land on a man-made island and that we have found oil and gas in that formation so quickly. Now the people of the north can be assured of a great future because we have found the way to drill efficiently and to protect the ecology at the same time.
Being the member of parliament for this area, he is not very well advised to come here today and tell me I was wrong when I got the permission of the people of Tuktoyaktuk to drill from a man-made island in very shallow water. There is no great problem there, such as there would be if you were drilling either from a platform or a ship in deep water. The drilling was in very shallow water and was carried out in accordance with regulations the government had put forward after studies had been carried out by my department, and after the advice of experts of the Department of the Environment and the people involved in the wildlife service had been given. So, Mr. Speaker, I think this is a great moment for the people of the north. They see that there is even more oil and gas there. This will help the economy of the north.
The hon. member raised the question of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. That pipeline is very important because it will mean that the resources in the north will some day be available for the Canadian market. The pipeline will not be used only for transportating American resources, Alaska, of course, being an American state. There is gas there which will go through the pipeline to the American market, but I hope at the same time that we can use that pipeline for Canadian resources we are finding in the north, resources which will meet the needs of Canadians. If there is enough there, perhaps we can sell some to the Americans. But if there is to be no pipeline, the resources we are finding in the north will not be available to Canadians. I therefore think that it is important for Canadians, because energy is so important.
We must utilize the resources we have. We have been drilling for them in a safe way on a man-made island built in shallow water in the Beaufort Sea. By so doing we are making sure that Canadian resources will be available for Canadians. These are resources for the south which come from the north. I therefore welcome this discovery by Imperial Oil, which came after drilling had been done in shallow water in the Beaufort Sea. The hon. member should be just as happy that we are proving to Canadians that the north is a great part of Canada.
